title: The Fathers on Leviticus
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The offering of tame animals pictures the saints, who die to the world and are offered through the Son as a fragrant sacrifice.
comments.comment: Is this not a clear type of the life of the saints, and of their complete closeness to God in spirit and sanctification? For we are pictured in the tame animals — the calf, I mean, and the sheep — dying to the world by putting the flesh to death, so that we may live to God through the Gospel way of life, and going up, as it were, as a sacrifice that is truly spiritual and most fragrant, offered through the Son to the Father.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The offering is brought to the doors of the tent because we are made acceptable to God only in the churches, where Christ brings us as priest, and the laying on of hands pictures our dying to the world.
comments.comment: It is brought to the very doors of the holy tent (Leviticus 1:3). For we are made perfect nowhere else than in the churches, since it is there, wholly and in every way, that we shall be acceptable to God the Father, with Christ as priest bringing us to him. For through him we have obtained access (Romans 5:2; Ephesians 2:18), and he himself opened for us the way in (Hebrews 10:19–20), entering the Holy of Holies as forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), and showing us the true path. God also commanded them to lay their hands on the calf (Leviticus 1:4), hinting at this indirectly: that in place of themselves they offer, in type, an image of our need to live in holiness by dying to the world, when they duly carry out the slaughter of the beast.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what bringing the offering to the doors and laying on hands signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The slaughter and the poured blood picture dying to the world and giving one's life to God, and the flaying and cutting show the word of God reaching into us.
comments.comment:
See, then, how the shadow gives shape to the truth for us. The calf was slaughtered before the Lord, and the blood was poured out on the altar (Leviticus 1:5). For dying to the world, and putting to death the impulses of the flesh, is most pleasing to God and worthy of his gaze from above. And perhaps our godly David sings of something like this when he says: ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones.’ (Psalm 116:15) For the death of the holy ones will be like a sacred offering to God; and surely I do not mean the death of all who live in the flesh. Rather, the word would point us to the death they are accustomed to endure, dying to the world but living to God in holiness and sanctification. For it is impossible for us to achieve the holy life unless we have first died to the world. For Peter writes about Christ: ‘He bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness.’ (1 Peter 2:24) So the slaughter of the calf seems to signify dying to sins, and enduring the death that is precious with God, the death he is pleased to look upon. For ‘they shall slaughter the calf,’ it says, ‘before the Lord.’ (Leviticus 1:5) And the pouring of the blood on the altar would signify, I think, the dedication of one's life and the offering up of the soul to the glory of God.

The victim is flayed and cut up limb by limb (Leviticus 1:6). The flaying suggests a kind of stripping bare and uncovering of what is within us; the cutting into pieces shows very well that the word of God reaches down to joints and marrow (Hebrews 4:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the slaughter, the blood and the cutting of the offering.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Everything of the saints is pleasing to God, and the parts laid on the altar stand for their life in the body, mind, thoughts and desires, and walk in deeds.
comments.comment: As the priest kindles the fire, the divided pieces are laid on the altar, with the head and the feet, and the entrails too, washed with water (Leviticus 1:7–9). For everything that belongs to the saints is fragrant, and nothing that is believed to be in them is rejected by God. The flesh would be a type of their life in the body, the coarser life, so to speak; for it is honorable and wholly pure. The head is a sign of the mind; the entrails stand for thoughts and desires; and the feet, in turn, are a subtle figure of the active life and of our walk, as it were, in deeds.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of the parts laid on the altar.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The lamb's slaughter on the north side of the altar shows that the flocks of the northern nations will also be holy to God.
comments.comment:
… ‘If his gift to the Lord,’ it says, ‘is from the flock, from the lambs or from the kids, for a whole burnt offering, he shall bring a male without blemish, and he shall lay his hand on its head, and they shall slaughter it at the side of the altar toward the north, before the Lord’ (Leviticus 1:10–11). This victim too is cut into pieces, and its entrails are washed, in the same way as the calf; and again he laid down that it must be carried up onto the altar (Leviticus 1:12–13). The meaning of the spiritual reading would be the same in this case as well. Yet there is one difference: the lamb was slaughtered at the side of the altar toward the north.

Palladius: What, then, is the meaning of this?

Cyril: Do you not know that the land of the Jews lies somewhat to the south, while the countless flocks of the nations have divided among themselves the regions toward the northern sea, settled in countries and cities?

Palladius: True.

Cyril: The sacrifice of the lamb in the more northern part, as it were, is therefore a figure showing that the flocks toward the north will also be holy to God. This is what the Savior too foretold about the flock from the nations, when he said: ‘And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and there will be one flock, one shepherd’ (John 10:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the north side of the altar is named.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The saints are like turtledoves and doves: gentle like Christ, speaking God's praise, holy in mind and life, and free of bodily indulgence.
comments.comment:
See again how finely and skillfully their likeness to Christ has been kept for the saints. For he himself is truly the most vocal turtledove, the one from above, and likewise the gentlest dove. Indeed, in the Song of Songs it is written of him: ‘The voice of the turtledove was heard in the wilderness’ (Song of Songs 2:12). And he set himself before us as a type and pattern of the greatest and highest gentleness, saying: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matthew 11:29). But see: because the saints themselves have come to be in the form of Christ, the beauty and the admirable worth found in goods that are, so to speak, the same have been well kept for them too. For they too may rightly be understood as turtledoves, since they send forth the divine and holy word to those who listen, and are eager to make songs and melodies for the glory of God. That is why they say: ‘My tongue shall tell of your righteousness, and of your praise all day long’ (Psalm 35:28). Moreover, they live out the life that is in Christ and hasten along the gentlest path of the Gospel way of life: to those who want to strike them on the right cheek they turn the left as well, and to those who press them into service for one mile they freely make a gift of going two, if those so choose (Matthew 5:39, 41). So they consecrate themselves to God as a fragrant aroma and as a whole burnt offering, in the form, as it were, of turtledoves and doves.

Then the priest wrings off the head and puts it on the altar, having poured out the blood (Leviticus 1:15). For the mind of the holiest saints is truly holy, and holy in the highest degree, and so it would be fitting for it to be dedicated to the wholly pure God. For it is full of good thoughts, and it gives off the fragrant ointment of the true knowledge of God; for, as it is written, ‘the thoughts of the righteous are just judgments’ (Proverbs 12:5). And that the life of those who live in the fear of God is holy too would become clear from the rule that the blood must be poured out at the holy altar; for the blood is a type of life.

The crop of the birds, that is, the craw, is removed together with the feathers, and it is thrown away as wholly useless. This too would be a clear sign that the life of the saints has been shown to stand above bodily indulgence, so that in a way it seems no longer to need even the stomach that holds the food. For such, in a way, is the life of those who labor most earnestly: paying no heed to food, and perhaps even to the stomach itself, they waste away the flesh and put pleasures to death, and they have become free and released from everything worldly and superfluous. This, I think, is what the casting away of the feathers means.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the birds, the head, the blood and the discarded crop of the bird offering stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Breaking the wings without dividing the bird pictures putting away arrogance and giving one's whole life undivided to God.
comments.comment: When the feathers have been plucked and the craw, that is, the crop, has been removed, ‘he shall break it,’ it says, ‘at the wings, and shall not divide it’ (Leviticus 1:17), and then he shall carry it up onto the altar. The breaking of the wings would be a type and a clear example of the mind of the saints not thinking proud thoughts, nor flying on high, but rather being drawn along with the lowly (Romans 12:16) and seeking, so to speak, the things below. For the mind of the arrogant is always lifted up somehow and carried toward the heights; it cannot bear to sit down with those of lower station, and it despises a modest and humble way of thinking. So the breaking of the wings shows in a figure the putting away of arrogance. And that it is not divided shows that they have dedicated their own life to God entirely and, if we may put it so, in every way, not divided toward the things of the world; and the wise Paul too said that those who are married are divided (1 Corinthians 7:33–34). Holy, then, is the mind of the saints, and holy their life: above bodily indulgence, free of worldly care, made beautiful by a modest mind, and undivided toward the things of the world. That is why it is dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the detail of the wings that are broken but not divided.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Fine flour, oil and frankincense picture a life given to God with cheerful hope and the fragrance of good works, so that we are remembered by him.
comments.comment: … That the fine flour is a type of life, the oil a type of the cheerfulness that belongs to hope, and the frankincense a type of the fragrance that comes from good works, upright deeds and a life fully in keeping with the law, we have explained at length already. So the law says that those who choose to make the God of all rejoice in them must by all means dedicate and consecrate their own life to him, without being gloomy over the sweat that virtue costs (‘Do not grumble,’ says the inspired Paul, 1 Corinthians 10:10), a life filled full of spiritual fragrance; for then the priest will offer up its memorial portion to God (Leviticus 2:2). For we shall draw near to God the Father in Christ through spiritual sacrifice, and gain this as well: to be kept in his remembrance. By the very things through which we are used to winning approval, we shall show that we are worthy of remembrance and that we have come to be known by God in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the flour, oil and frankincense and the memorial portion mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The law accepts even the cheapest offering from oven, pan or grill if it has oil and frankincense, as Christ accepts a cup of cold water.
comments.comment: What deserves our attention here, I think, is the law’s forethought and great skill. You will certainly see it: it accepts what is very small indeed, and to that too it grants, in every case, fragrance and cheerfulness. For you have surely heard Christ himself say: ‘And whoever gives one of these brothers, the little ones, a cup of cold water to drink, only in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward’ (Matthew 10:42). We must reason in some such way here too, and applaud the Lawgiver’s kindness with the praises that befit him. For, as I said, he accepts the offering even if someone chooses to fulfill what is prescribed with the very cheapest things. For whether it is a loaf, the law says, or a single wafer, whether from the oven or from the pan or indeed from the grill, and even if it is not of wheat at all but groats and crushed grain, that is, meal made from pulse, let what is brought be moistened with oil, and let it in turn have frankincense lavished on it. And in these very details the passage seems somehow to hint to us at the approval the saints win through fiery trial and toil, and indeed through being crushed.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Leaven and honey are not offered on the altar because shrewdness and sweetness may be either good or bad, yet they may be brought as firstfruits.
comments.comment: Leaven, then, would be a type of shrewdness, and not by any means only of the kind that is blamed, but of the other kind too, I mean the good kind that is praised, which the word of Wisdom also promises to give to the innocent (Proverbs 1:4). For the word ‘shrewdness’ is, in a sense, neutral. Honey, in turn, sometimes hints to us indirectly at bodily pleasure, as in the saying: ‘Do not give heed to a worthless woman; for honey drips from the lips of a prostitute’ (Proverbs 5:3). But at other times it gives a picture of good sweetness. For it is written: ‘Eat honey, my son, for the honeycomb is good, that your throat may be sweetened’ (Proverbs 24:13). So the law forbids that leaven and honey be brought for a burnt offering and sacrifice. It accepts them from the one who brings them as a gift and as firstfruits, but by no means carries them up for a fragrant aroma to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why leaven and honey may be brought as firstfruits but not burned on the altar.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The salt on the sacrifice shows that we must approach God consecrated with understanding.
comments.comment: The sacrifice was sprinkled with salt, the type signifying that one must be consecrated to God with understanding, and make one’s approach to him, as it were, most savoury. For bread will not be eaten without salt, as it is written (Job 6:6). Christ said to the holy apostles: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the salt on the sacrifice.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: A peace offering must be without blemish, and the fat on the entrails stands for the good health of the mind nourished by the Spirit.
comments.comment: The calf, then, is without blemish; for it is fitting that those who go up to God as a fragrant aroma should be pure and keep as far as they can from every blemish. It was slaughtered at the very doors of the holy tent, with the hands of the one offering it laid upon it; and what this means has been plainly stated already. The fat on the entrails was carried up for sacrifice, and the two kidneys, with the fat in them removed along with them, and the lobe of the liver. The fat on the entrails, I think, would signify the good health, so to speak, of the mind, and the richness of the inner parts when they have been nourished as well as can be on the spiritual provisions given through the Spirit. For good feeding makes brute animals, and human bodies too, grow fat; but a most abundant share in divine gifts fills the mind of the saints with every good thing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The kidneys stand for the mind's discernment and the lobe of the liver for its desires, and both are to be dedicated to God.
comments.comment:
The kidneys, again, would be a type of the activity of discernment within the mind, by which one rejects what by nature does harm, and counts what is beneficial as worth choosing and taking. And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Test all things; hold fast what is good; keep away from every form of evil’ (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). So since the kidney is a part of the body that discerns (for it separates out what is surplus very well, lets what is wholesome and useful into the body, and distributes it with art to the parts that should receive it, and in the right amount), we must with good reason take the kidneys to mean the discernment of the mind. Holy, then, and an offering dedicated to God are the kidneys of the saints, that is, the discernment they have in the mind. For those who cleave to God are approved and exact money changers: they always reject what is worthless as counterfeit, but they are accustomed to honor with their excellent verdict whatever leads to benefit. It was in this way, I think, that the inspired Psalmist, who was used to winning approval, cried out to God: ‘For you have taken possession of my kidneys, O Lord’ (Psalm 139:13).

The lobe of the liver, for its part, points us to nothing other than an activity of the soul, that is, a movement of the mind, by which it reaches out toward desires. Some who have studied such matters closely say without hesitation that every living creature has its desires in the liver. So the lobe of the liver too must be dedicated to God, that is, so to speak, the very source of all our desire, as the Psalmist sings: ‘Lord, all my desire is before you’ (Psalm 38:9). And a person takes pride in himself and sings out so solemn and admirable a word if his longings are set on nothing but what pleases God, and he is found thirsting for whatever he himself may wish to do.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the kidneys and the lobe of the liver offered to God stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Calf, sheep and goat mark different measures of fruitfulness among believers, and God will repay each according to his deeds.
comments.comment: For the sheep, in turn, and for the goat as well, the Lawgiver lays down the same law, and the sacrifice was carried out in the same way for these too (Leviticus 3:6–16). The difference in size among the animals neatly points to the measure of piety and approval among those who are used to bearing fruit. For one person, we should think, bears fruit richly and above the rest, as in the calf; another moderately, as in the sheep; and another more modestly still, for a goat is smaller than a sheep. And this, I think, is the fruitful earth yielding a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold, as in the parable in the Gospels (Matthew 13:8). … That the repayment of reward will be in proportion to each one’s good deeds, and that God will allot to those who have chosen to act nobly rewards matched to their labors, the Savior himself will assure us. He says that the talents were not handed out in equal shares (Matthew 25:15), and of those who did well he sets one over ten cities and another over five (Luke 19:17–19). For each one’s life is weighed, as it were, in the balance, and the repayment will surely be equal in weight to our goodness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The unblemished calf is a type of Christ, who bore no wound of sin and was offered before the Lord at the doors of the holy tent for the Church.
comments.comment: The calf, then, is taken without blemish and without wound (Leviticus 4:3) as a type of Christ, who is truly without blemish and did not submit to the wound that sin inflicts. ‘For the ruler of this world is coming,’ he says, ‘and he will find nothing in me’ (John 14:30); for he committed no sin, as the Scriptures say (1 Peter 2:22). And it is brought to the very doors of the holy tent, before the Lord (Leviticus 4:4); so Christ, as it were, did not refuse to suffer for the holy tent, that is, the Church, and was dedicated for her as a fragrant aroma to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2). That is why he said, ‘For their sake I sanctify myself’ (John 17:19). By ‘I sanctify’ he means ‘I bring and dedicate an unblemished offering to God the Father.’ For whatever is dedicated to God is said to be sanctified, as in the saying somewhere in Scripture: ‘It is a snare to a man to sanctify hastily something of his own, for after he has made the vow he comes to regret it’ (Proverbs 20:25). The words ‘before the Lord’ show that the offering is acceptable and well pleasing. For we already know what is written about the pair of brothers, I mean Cain and Abel: ‘God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts,’ it says, ‘but to Cain and his sacrifices he paid no heed’ (Genesis 4:4–5). For it is plain enough that God looks upon what pleases him, and turns away in hatred from what does not. When the hands of the one who has sinned have been laid on the calf, the slaughter is carried out, and that before the Lord (Leviticus 4:4). For ‘he takes away our sins and suffers pain for us’ (Isaiah 53:4) as he is slain; for the hand stands as a type of deeds and actions. Yet he is slain before the Lord, the Father all but consenting that the Son must die for us. For the Father does not turn away when he sees him slain; not that he in any way praises the suffering, but he knows well that Emmanuel’s suffering for us brings salvation to the world. So it is he who takes away our sins and suffers pain for us (Isaiah 53:4), enduring for our sake the slaughter on the precious cross.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the unblemished calf and its slaughter before the Lord stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The blood sprinkled seven times before the veil and put on the altar's horns shows Christ as atonement and mercy seat, whose death is a fragrance of life.
comments.comment: Then the priest takes some of the blood on his finger and sprinkles it seven times on the holy veil (Leviticus 4:6), which was over the ark, and whose name is the mercy seat. He also smears the horns of the altar of incense (Leviticus 4:7). For Christ has become for us both atonement (1 John 2:2) and mercy seat (Romans 3:25). Yet it is in the blood of an eternal covenant (Hebrews 13:20) that he grants us the most perfect cleansing. This, I think, is the meaning of the mercy seat being sprinkled seven times with the blood, for the number seven is a sign of perfection. For his death too is fragrant with the salvation and life of the world, and with our access to God in faith. ‘For one died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised’ (2 Corinthians 5:14–15), as the Scriptures say. So the smearing of the golden altar of incense with the blood shows the fragrance of his death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the blood sprinkled seven times and put on the horns of the incense altar.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ, slaughtered at the doors of the tent, sanctifies the Church by the sprinkling of his own blood, which speaks better things than Abel's.
comments.comment: He it is who sanctifies the Church by the sprinkling of his own blood, and does so abundantly. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger before the Lord’ (Leviticus 4:6). ‘For we have come,’ it says, ‘to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than Abel’ (Hebrews 12:22–24). Abel’s blood cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), condemning the murderer; but the precious blood of Christ, the Savior of us all, speaks better things to God on our behalf, for it was poured out as the price given in exchange for the life of all. The blood of the calf was poured out at the base of the altar, for the death of Christ is truly holy and sacred.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The inner parts offered on the altar are the hidden virtues of Christ, while the body burned outside the camp shows him suffering outside the gate to cleanse the defiled.
comments.comment: When the inner parts of the calf have been taken out and carried up to the altar (Leviticus 4:8–10), the rest of the body is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:11–12). For he himself is the holy sacrifice, fragrant with virtues, of which the inner parts would be types, since the virtues are hidden, as it were, within us and lie deep within the mind. He is also the one who suffers outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), and by the death of his own flesh cleanses those who were defiled. For ‘the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on those who are defiled,’ it says, ‘sanctify for the purification of the flesh’ (Hebrews 9:13). So Emmanuel, being one and the same, gives off his fragrance in the holy tents, I mean the churches, and he also suffered outside the gate; and there, as the inspired Paul said, we too must go out, bearing his reproach (Hebrews 13:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the rest of the sin offering is burned outside the camp.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The same calf is brought for the people's sins, because Christ offered himself alike for small and great.
comments.comment: A calf is also brought for the sins of ignorance of the people (Leviticus 4:13–14), in the same way and without any difference, and the meaning of the sacrifice was the same in every case. For Emmanuel offered himself in the same way for small and great, for people and priests alike.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: In the bull slain for the congregation we see Christ slain for us, freeing us from sin, and the projecting horns of the altar are a figure of the cross.
comments.comment: But see Emmanuel again, slain for us as in the bull, freeing us from sin, taking us out of the reach of judgment and carrying us away from punishment, and passing through the greater and more perfect tent, not by bulls and goats but by his own blood (Hebrews 9:11–12), having tasted death once for all. For up on the wood, when his side was pierced with a spear, he poured out blood and water (John 19:34). And the projecting horns would be a figure of the cross, as we said before.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The victims match the size of the sin: one calf for ruler and people sick with a common sin, one goat for one soul, while Christ offered himself for all together.
comments.comment: Do you see, Palladius, the depth of the mystery, sketched for the people of old as in a mirror and in shadows? For the bringing of victims matches, as it were, the size of the transgressions. A calf was offered for ruler and people alike, perhaps because the two had been sick with one common sin; but one kid for one, that is, for one soul. For Christ offered himself for all together, as is pictured in the calf, a weighty and great victim: ‘For where sin abounded,’ it says, ‘grace abounded all the more’ (Romans 5:20).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The male goat for a ruler and the female for one of the people show that the cleansing through Christ is in proportion to each one's fault, since rulers are liable to greater charges.
comments.comment: But if the one guilty of the offenses happened to be a ruler, the goat was male (Leviticus 4:22–23); if, however, it was one of the people, a single person, the victim was female, whether it happened to be a sheep or from the goats (Leviticus 4:27–32). Even in the difference between the victims the law points to the wisdom of our Savior’s plan of salvation. For the male always in some way leads and holds first honor, while the female follows and stands second. So the cleansing through Christ is in proportion to each one’s faults, both in those who preside and lead and in those under their authority, each individual subject. For when ruler and people fall into sin they would not be liable to equal charges; the rulers, surely, to greater ones. That is why they are scoured clean by a richer grace.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The law counts the man who ignores an adjuration as guilty as one with other defilements or perjury, and release comes through confession and above all through the death of Christ.
comments.comment:
Observe, then, that the law sets in one equal and identical class of offense the man who hears the voice of adjuration and makes nothing at all of the matter, the man liable for other defilements, and, besides these, the man condemned for perjury. For contempt toward God is truly a monstrous defilement, and it rises to the very extreme of evil; and this offense is near and akin to the uncleannesses of the flesh. Or must we not count accursed perjury and contempt for adjuration as equal?

Palladius: Certainly; for in both cases the charges are always, in a way, evenly matched.

Cyril: Then for these also release will follow through confession and through the slaying of a ewe lamb, that is, a sheep. For, it says, ‘Be the first to tell your lawless deeds, that you may be justified’ (Isaiah 43:26). And the divine David also cries out: ‘I said, I will confess my lawlessness against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart’ (Psalm 32:5). Yet confession alone is not enough to wash us completely clean. It is the death of Christ that sets us entirely free, for he suffered for us and put himself under the sins of us all, as in every kind of domestic animal: I mean in the calf, and in the sheep and the goat.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Where a man cannot afford a sheep the law accepts birds, and the turtledove and the dove are fitting types of Christ, with his sweet voice and his meekness.
comments.comment: And the law, as if to leave those in defilements and uncleannesses no excuse for neglecting sacrifice, urges anyone who has no calf or sheep to give honor with what is at hand and within his means, saying: … We should compare our Lord Jesus Christ, and very fittingly, to the turtledove and the dove, because the one has the sweetest voice and is the most vocal of birds, and the other comes nearest to the height of meekness. Both were in Christ. For he, the turtledove from above and from heaven, charmed the whole world with the preaching of the Gospel, sending forth, as it were, a clear and sweet song, and making plain the will of God the Father. For as the inspired John says: ‘He whom God has sent speaks the words of God’ (John 3:34). And he also called us to imitate the meekness and gentleness that were in him …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The bird is nipped but its head not cut off, to show that the death of Christ brings union and not division, and that he is both sin offering and burnt offering for us.
comments.comment: The priest, then, it says, will take the turtledove and nip it with his fingernail (Leviticus 5:8), for that is how light birds are killed. Yet he will not cut it off completely; he clearly means the head. For so the death of Christ was accomplished, not for division but for union. That is why at the beginning, too, when he laid down the law for the Passover, he commanded that the lamb be sacrificed, and yet, he says, ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside’ (Exodus 12:46). For Christ is in no way divided (1 Corinthians 1:13); he is one, whole in each and in all. And he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), gathering us into union, both with one another in oneness of soul and, through himself, with God in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). That the death of Christ has brought us not division but union, the bird showed indirectly by being sacrificed without its head being cut clean off the neck. And that he sanctifies the Church with his own blood (Hebrews 13:12) would be signified by the sprinkling of the tent and the things in it with the bird’s blood. One turtledove is for sin, and one, again, for a whole burnt offering; and through both Christ is understood, both dying for us and being offered to the Father as a whole burnt offering for a fragrant aroma (Ephesians 5:2), and offering himself up as the exchange for the life of all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the bird's head is not cut off and why there are two birds.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Fine flour for sin has no oil or frankincense because sin has no gladness or fragrance, and it signifies the life of the one who offers.
comments.comment: The law, moreover, brings the form of the sacrifice down to something very easy to obtain, and commands that it be made in proportion to each person’s means. In this way it cuts away at every point any hesitation over the best offerings, and leaves those who choose slackness without excuse. … But in these provisions the manner of the sacrifice no longer points to Christ; it hints to us at the life of the one who offers, his approach in Christ, and his consecration to God. For fine flour is offered, the substance from which bread is made, and bread is a type of life. But the law says that it must not be sprinkled with frankincense, nor moistened with oil (Leviticus 5:11), and quite rightly it states beforehand the wise and necessary reason for this: that it is for sin. From sin, gladness, which is understood in the oil, would be utterly and in every way far removed, and so would fragrance, which is perhaps understood in the frankincense. It could not be disputed that the sin in us is truly a gloomy and scentless thing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sin offering of flour has no oil or frankincense.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: A life without gladness and fragrance is changed in Christ, for through him we offer to the Father no longer ourselves but Christ who is in us.
comments.comment: So the fine flour without frankincense and oil is a type of a life that has no gladness and is bare of fragrance; but in Christ even this life will be changed to gladness. It also receives fragrance in faith and is offered to God through him who scours clean the defiled and spiritually washes those caught in uncleanness. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall take a handful of the fine flour and carry it up to the altar of whole burnt offerings to the Lord’ (Leviticus 5:12). For our approach is in Christ, and through him we who are defiled draw near (Ephesians 2:18). We are justified through faith, and as a pleasing fragrance we offer up to the Father no longer ourselves, but Christ who is in us (Galatians 2:20), since we have the spiritual fragrance (2 Corinthians 2:15).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Stealing consecrated things or failing to pay a vow is dreadful, and it is forgiven by repayment with a fifth added and the ram, a type of Christ.
comments.comment: Besides this, if it should happen that some offend God and steal something of what has been consecrated, or go back on what they promised and do not offer it at once, and so through carelessness in these matters incur the charge of forgetfulness, the law cleanses this too. … For it is truly a dreadful thing to steal anything of what has been consecrated and dedicated to the glory of God. In the same way, and on no small charges, failure to pay what was promised will be denounced. For ‘My son,’ it says, ‘if you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay to pay it; it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay’ (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). And the divinely inspired David sings somewhere: ‘Make vows, and pay them to the Lord your God’ (Psalm 76:11). The sons of Eli too were punished for pilfering some of the holy things and taking for themselves what belonged to God (1 Samuel 2:12–17). What, then, might be the forgiveness for this as well? Or how might one free his foot from the charge and be set free? First, if he makes the repayment richer than what was stolen (‘For he shall add the fifth,’ it says); then, if he brings a purchased ram for sacrifice. This would be a type of Christ, whom the leaders of the Jews in a sense bought for thirty denarii, which they paid to the disciple who betrayed him (Matthew 26:15). So in Christ there is forgiveness for offenses against God as well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the added fifth and the ram for wrongs done in holy things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The law makes the man who consumes holy things through forgetfulness or ignorance repay it with a fifth added, and those who handle sacred things must not claim any for themselves.
comments.comment: But if anyone kept back the whole gift entirely for himself and spent it on his own needs, having burned none of it, he was charged under the law as one who had eaten holy things. This is just what the sons of Eli the priest did: they seized and profaned the sacred offerings before the sacrifices were made, and said most impiously to those who came to sacrifice, ‘Give meat for the priest to roast’ (1 Samuel 2:15). But those deeds, being deliberate and plainly insolent, were punished accordingly. ‘But if,’ he says, ‘someone, either overtaken by forgetfulness or not knowing exactly what the laws require, should do any such thing, let him bear a penalty: let him repay the same amount without fail, and let him add to it a fifth as well,’ that is, the fifth part of the value; ‘for in this way he will be cleared of the charges and will ward off the harm that comes from ignorance’ (Leviticus 22:14; Leviticus 5:15–16). If, then, what is done in ignorance is not free from indictment, what would anyone think of what is done out of madness and audacity? Those, then, who have the care of the sacred things must refrain from seeking to claim anything for themselves before the sacrifice; otherwise let them know that, having committed grave offenses, they will incur punishment and come under the wrath of God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The law requires both repayment with increase to the wronged brother and a ram for God, and whoever would have Christ dwell in him must first wash away his offenses by making amends.
comments.comment: Do you see how the way of cleansing runs alike in both cases and is completed by both means? For he repays with increase, and he brings a ram. The law very rightly commanded that offenses against God and offenses against brothers and kinsmen alike must be put away. But justification in Christ is by no means partial; it is rather a complete washing away of whatever tends to stain us. Therefore he also said: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life’ (John 5:24). If, then, the one who through Christ has justification by faith conferred on him has escaped being judged, we are bound to say that he has escaped the charges; and no kind of accusation, I say, could prevail against such a person. For ‘it is God who justifies; who is he that condemns?’ (Romans 8:33–34). So when we answer with deeds to those brothers who have been grieved, we shall find justification in Christ close at hand. … For I think that those who are to make Christ dwell within themselves through the Spirit (Ephesians 3:16–17) must first wash off their filth and first scour away their offenses, and so show him their own soul bright and spotless, just as the divinely inspired Psalmist, having reached this fine state of virtue, cried aloud: ‘My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody’ (Psalm 57:7). For just as dyes settle into wool when it is clean, but if any trace of dirt remains, what was taken in is at once easily shed and finds no firm hold in it, so too participation in Christ sinks into holy and pure souls, but would not settle at all in those that are not so. ‘For the Holy Spirit of wisdom will flee from deceit,’ as it is written, ‘and will not dwell in a body in debt to sins’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4–5). So by making amends to those who have been wronged, and by good deeds that lead to friendship and shear away our brothers’ grief, we shall free ourselves from every charge and gain the forgiveness that is in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The altar's fire is never put out and is its own, from heaven, and it points to Christ, the true altar through whom we offer spiritual worship.
comments.comment:
The fire of the altar, then, is continual and wholly unceasing; and it is not foreign or brought from outside, but its own, that is, the fire that is from above and from heaven. And what does this mean? Our holy altar is filled with the glory of God, and the divine and ineffable nature is pictured in the form of fire. But the passage also seems to hint, and very aptly, at something mystical.

Palladius: What do you mean by that?

Cyril: Were we not saying that Emmanuel himself is, as in a type, the divine altar, through whom we draw near to God the Father, offering spiritual worship and all but sacrificing the fragrance of the virtues and the holiness of the gospel way of life? For ‘present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship.’ (Romans 12:1)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The ash must be carried out by the priest himself, because nothing of divine service is too lowly to hand to someone who is not holy.
comments.comment: But he adds a further command that is useful at the literal level as well. He says the ash must be carried out not by someone else, an outsider, that is, someone of another tribe, but rather by the service of those who have been sanctified (Leviticus 6:10–11). Observe how the law allows nothing that belongs to divine service to be thought trivial, or unworthy, as it were, of the priest’s own hands, so that he might hand it over to someone else who is not holy; for the holy things are not open to the unclean. The divine altar itself, too, is not to be touched.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the priest himself must carry out the ash.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The fire that stays always on the altar pictures the Holy Spirit remaining on Christ, and the believer who has dedicated his life should likewise be warm and fervent in the Spirit.
comments.comment: Consider, then, that the law does not allow the fire that came down from heaven upon the altar to die down, or, as it were, to fade and go away, but has it stay on the altar always and make its home there without ceasing (Leviticus 6:12–13). And John the Baptist bore witness about Christ: ‘I have seen the Spirit descending from heaven in the form of a dove, and it remained on him. And I did not know him,’ he says, ‘but he who sent me to baptize said to me: He on whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining on him, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit’ (John 1:32–33). So the Holy Spirit was being prefigured, still as in shadows, coming down upon Christ in the form of fire and always remaining on him. For the fire of the altar never sleeps and never ceases at all. That the Spirit is likened to the nature of fire, the blessed Baptist also assures you when he says to the crowds of the Jews: ‘I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie’ (John 1:26–27). And he said: ‘He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire’ (Matthew 3:11). For we have been baptized not into fire that the senses perceive, but in the Holy Spirit, who like fire melts away the defilement in souls. That is why it is also written of Christ: ‘Behold, he comes in like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap; and he will sit refining and cleansing, as silver and as gold’ (Malachi 3:2–3). The fire of the altar, then, cannot be quenched. For the Holy Spirit has remained in Christ, even though the Spirit is in him by nature, inasmuch as he is God and is understood to be God. The law also called the fire the altar’s own (Leviticus 6:9). For even though the Only-begotten became man, and in the manner fitting for humanity is also said to have come to share in the Spirit, the Spirit is nonetheless both his and in him, and truly his own. But if someone chooses to apply this passage to each of those sanctified through faith in Christ, so that each is in some way already understood to be a divine altar, the reading is a profitable one. For it is fitting that holy men, who have dedicated their own life to Christ, be seen warm and fervent in the Spirit (Romans 12:11), and always so: not sinking into coldness through worldly pleasures, but rather rekindling the mind in holiness toward love of God and desire for virtue. For this is the manner of rational worship (Romans 12:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the altar fire that must never go out stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The handful of fine flour with oil and frankincense pictures a life that is fragrant and hopeful but divided between God and the world, and Christ brings such a life to God for remembrance.
comments.comment:
An exact figure of this life is the fine flour offered up in the priest’s handful with the oil and the frankincense. For the life consecrated to God, even if perhaps only in part, must surely be fragrant, and enriched with the richest hopes. Or would you not say that every good work of ours is most fragrant?

Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: What then? Is it not done by us in good hope?

Palladius: Yes, for what comes from God will surely follow.

Cyril: So the frankincense, and the fine flour moistened with oil, point us to a life that is fragrant and very rich.

Palladius: Well said. But what kind of life among us would be holy in part?

Cyril: One that has not reached the goal of a saintly way of life, and does not walk the path set very high, as perhaps John did, he who was the voice, or the holy apostles; and yet one that does not lose its claim to reverence merely because it perhaps falls short of the lofty path set before us. Or is not the life of those in the world who have children, if they choose to live uprightly, in some way divided between God and the world, in the words of blessed Paul (1 Corinthians 7:33–34)?

Palladius: It is divided; how could it not be?

Cyril: So the partial consecration of the fine flour, which has fragrance and cheerfulness, was a type of the life that is not wholly given over to God, but stands in the middle, as it were, and looks both ways. The law says that this will also be for a memorial (Leviticus 6:15) of the one who brought it through the ministry of the priest. And truly we shall gain this: to be held in God’s remembrance through the things by which we bear fruit and give off fragrance. For Christ acts as mediator and brings to God both the one who is wholly holy, as one ranked among the whole burnt offerings, and the one who is not entirely so, because he is divided and given in part to the world, as a kind of partial offering.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: What is done for God should be unleavened, free of any wish to please men, and the male's eating the portion shows that softness is unholy in those God has chosen.
comments.comment: The grain offering is unleavened. For it is fitting that whatever we do be done with purity, for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). Indeed, the Savior commanded us to shun standing in the middle of the marketplaces to make our prayers (Matthew 6:5), a gloomy face when fasting (Matthew 6:16), and sounding a trumpet unbecomingly when we show mercy to our brothers (Matthew 6:2). For this is leaven, which profanes holy things. What is done for the glory of God should be free of any charge of seeking to please men; for in this way the offering would be truly unleavened and holy. The remainder of the grain offering is a portion and food for the priests. Every male eats it in a holy place (Leviticus 6:16–18). That the holy things are consumed by the priests in a holy place preserves the reverence due to our more mystical teachings; that every male eats it aptly suggests that softness is an ugly thing, and truly unholy, in those whom God has chosen. For softness makes a man unholy, cuts him off from spiritual blessing, and leaves him without share in the good things God has allotted to the saints.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The priests' offering is made wholly, morning and evening, because the chosen man is undivided and always fragrant to God, with a heart easily broken.
comments.comment:
See, Palladius, how exact the law is, and how finely it provides for the safety proper to holy things. Since he commanded that the offerings of the common flock should not be wholly burnt, because these people do not have a life that is entirely holy, but one divided, as it were, between God and the world, he rightly makes a distinction: he places those chosen for sacred service in the higher rank, and says that the offering made for them must be wholly burnt, as they burn to God as incense the fine flour that is brought, morning and evening, that is, through the whole day and at every season. For the chosen man is always, in some sense, holy, and has a fragrance that never ceases, a spiritual one, clearly. He is not divided between God and the world, as some are, but is in constant attendance and without distraction (1 Corinthians 7:35), wholly and entirely devoted to his own Master, and crying out, as it were: ‘I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me’ (Galatians 2:20).

The tenth of the fine flour, then, would be a sign of a life that gives off fragrance to God at every season. But ‘in a pan,’ he says, and ‘kneaded with oil,’ and ‘he shall bring it in broken pieces’ (Leviticus 6:21). In a veiled way these signify to us: the pan, I think, what is painful; the kneading with oil, abundance joined with cheerfulness; the broken pieces, the tender and, so to speak, easily broken heart of the saints. For the life that is entirely and wholly holy will surely have to be lived amid toils, will have abundant hope in God, and will have a heart very easily broken; for hardness would least befit it. For it is written: ‘A broken and humbled heart God will not despise’ (Psalm 51:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the priests' grain offering is wholly burned, and its pan, oil and broken pieces.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The sin offering can be only Christ, holy altogether, and eating it in the holy court pictures the holy table of the churches.
comments.comment:
The victim for sin, then, could be none other than Emmanuel, who is the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). And he is slaughtered in the place of the whole burnt offering. For Christ is not holy in part, as we are, for he committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22); he is wholly fragrant and sacred, and the giver of holiness to all others. For even if he was reckoned among the lawless (Isaiah 53:12) and, in the divine plan, was counted among the condemned, the Father knows the death of the Son to be holy and sacred. That is why he says: ‘In the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offering, they shall slaughter the sin offering also; it is most holy’ (Leviticus 6:25). For just as the Son is God of gods, so also is he Holy of holies, himself making the whole creation holy by his own Spirit, since he is by nature from the Father and is truly God.

The priest who brings the sacrifice, he says, shall eat it. For each one, I think, who has been brought into the sacred ministry will gather the fruit of his own labors and reap the reward of his own service. And what remains of the sacrifice is eaten in holy places and in the court of the holy tent (Leviticus 6:26). For the mysteries are offered in churches, and in them the chosen race is counted worthy of the holy table of Christ. And wherever a lawful priest serves, the place will be holy. And the sacrifice makes holy the one who touches it, and so does the sprinkling of the blood (Leviticus 6:27).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sin offering is killed in the place of the burnt offering and is most holy.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The sin offerings are eaten only by the priests, because the holy body of Christ is to be shared only by chosen and pure souls.
comments.comment: Again, he gives the name ‘sins’ to the victims slain for sins. These too would be types of Christ, who was sacrificed for us and endured the slaughter in order to abolish the sin of the world (John 1:29). And the offerings for sin may be eaten only by those who perform the sacred rites (Leviticus 6:26, 29). For it is fitting that the holy body of Christ be shared not by unholy souls but by chosen and pure ones, to whom one might apply the words, ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession’ (1 Peter 2:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Vessels that served the sacrifices are purified so that they are not put to human use.
comments.comment: And the vessels that serve the sacrifices are also purified (Leviticus 6:28), so that what has served sacred things may belong to nothing else and not be put to human uses. This law has been kept, and it is preserved in the churches. And the law will again make clear that being blessed befits those who act with manly courage, when it says: ‘Every male among the priests shall eat them’ (Leviticus 6:29).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The inward parts of the victims must not be made into food but be burned, as dedicated to the divine nature alone, of which fire is a type.
comments.comment: For he declares that the inward parts of the victims must not be made into food. They must, he says, be dedicated to God alone and offered to him. This, I think, is what ‘it shall be burned up in fire’ points to; that is, what is dedicated is to be plainly assigned to the divine nature alone, which is above all things, and of which fire is a type.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The blood poured at the altar's base and the inward parts offered up point to Christ's holy death and to many kinds of virtue.
comments.comment: And when the ram of the guilt offering is sacrificed, its blood is poured out at the base of the altar; for the death of Christ is holy and sacred, and fragrant as well. For the inward parts are offered up: the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver. These, I think, as I have said elsewhere too, would be a type of virtue, not of one virtue only but of many kinds. For the ways of virtue are very many. And so we have been justified in Christ, who endured death for us and dedicated himself to God the Father as a fragrant aroma (Ephesians 5:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The priests' equal shares are still kept in the churches, giving those who serve at the altar each his portion.
comments.comment: This law too is preserved in the churches, and it secures equality for those who serve at the altar, giving each, without variation, his portion of the bloodless sacrifice. Knowing this, Paul writes: ‘So also the Lord commanded that those who attend the altar should live from the altar’ (1 Corinthians 9:13–14). And those who offer the sacrifices are sharers in the altar, as he himself says again somewhere (1 Corinthians 10:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the equal shares given to the priests.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The law commands leavened loaves for the sacrifice of praise though it forbids leaven elsewhere, and this praise is offered by many together in the churches and by one alone at home, with no distinction among them.
comments.comment:
He has commanded that the sacrifice of praise be made with leavened loaves, even though elsewhere he said clearly and plainly: ‘You shall offer no leaven and no honey to the Lord your God. You shall offer them to the Lord as a gift of firstfruits, but they shall not be put on the altar for a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Leviticus 2:11–12). … What, then, is the meaning of this arrangement? Come, let us say, searching it out as far as we can and opening up the hidden path. So, very much in keeping with the law, the inspired David too, striking up the spiritual lyre, says: ‘I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord’ (Psalm 116:13), and so expressly calls the sacrifice of praise a cup of salvation. And we too offer praise in great numbers in the churches, in unity of spirit, brought together through faith as into one body (Ephesians 4:3–4) and one soul. For it is written: ‘The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul’ (Acts 4:32). We also often give glory alone, quietly at home, by day and by night; and this is the habit of good people. Or is what I say not true?

Palladius: How could it not be?

Cyril: But whether the offering is brought by us in the churches in great numbers, or is performed in other places, perhaps by one alone, or by two somewhere, or three, or more still, no distinction is drawn among those present who are accustomed to sing hymns and have gathered for this.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Leavened bread and unleavened wafers in the sacrifice of praise stand for the unbaptized and the cleansed lives, and the fine flour and oil for praise given alone and with gladness.
comments.comment: This is why the law did well to foretell this arrangement, when it commanded that the sacrifice of praise be made with leavened loaves and with unleavened wafers (Leviticus 7:12–13). Each of the things named, I think, points to a kind of life. The leavened bread will be a type of a life not yet cleansed through holy baptism, nor yet wholly freed from the world’s uncleanness. The unleavened wafer is a type of the life already washed clean in Christ through faith: the life of the perfect, I mean, whom the inspired Paul also addressed when he said: ‘Let us therefore keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth’ (1 Corinthians 5:8). And again: ‘So cleanse out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). … Besides these, the fine flour, not yet brought together into one mass as it is in a loaf or a wafer, but still remaining, as it were, in its grains, hints that each of those who offer the praise does so as one by himself. For we are acceptable to God when we give him glory both each of us on our own and all of us together as one company. Oil is poured on the sacrifice of praise, signifying the gladness of the act, and that mercy from God will in every way and without fail follow those who are accustomed to offer it. For it says: ‘Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me’ (Psalm 50:14–15). And the disciple of Christ also writes: ‘Is anyone among you downcast? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise’ (James 5:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the thank offering includes both leavened bread and unleavened wafers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The priests' share shows the priesthood is rewarded, and the command to eat on the day it is offered hints that a new way of giving glory will be devised when this age has passed.
comments.comment: One portion of each was brought forward (Leviticus 7:14), and of the fine flour, as it were, a single handful; a sheep was slaughtered and its inner parts were burnt according to the law; and the rest was food for those appointed to serve as priests, the law thus showing that the priesthood does not go unrewarded. And it adds a further command: ‘On the day it is offered it shall be eaten; they shall not leave any of it until the morning’ (Leviticus 7:15). Through this, again, we may perhaps understand something like this: when the time has run its course, and the present age has passed like a day, another manner of giving glory, beyond those we know, will be devised for us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Worship that clings to the shadows of the law is rejected, like flesh left to the third day, now that Christ has come and ended the law.
comments.comment: The law has shown us many times already in what came before that divine Scripture is accustomed to divide the whole of time sometimes into two: the time when the law was in force, and the time when Christ shone forth; and sometimes again into three, inserting and placing between them the time when the choir of the holy prophets shone forth; except that in the time of Moses and in that of the holy prophets the manner of worship was the same, since it was still in the shadows of the law. But when morning has come, that is, when the third season has at last been revealed in turn, and the spiritual light, that is, Christ, shines all around the world beneath the sun, and the ancient mist has at last been dispersed, the manner of worship of that former time is no longer acceptable. Whether the fat or the sacrifice is yesterday’s or the third day’s, it is no longer acceptable, but loathsome and rejected before God, and counted as a defilement for those who choose to bring it out of season. … So it is sin and defilement, now that Christ has been revealed and the time of the law and the prophets has gone by, to cling to worship as in shadows, and to attempt to bring to God a sheep, or fat, or frankincense, even though the Son says plainly to God the Father: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said: See, I have come, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book, to do your will, O God’ (Hebrews 10:5–7; Psalm 40:6–8). For the Son, offering himself up for us as a spotless victim (Hebrews 9:14), put a stop to the things of the law, which could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:11); for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets (Romans 10:4).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The tent and altar are holy through the sanctifying Spirit and contact with the sacrifice, as any place where Christ is present is holy.
comments.comment: For the tent is holy, and the altar is fully enriched with the sanctification that comes through the Spirit, though it does not share in it as one ranked among rational beings does; for it is not holy in the way that, say, the nature of an angel or a human soul is holy, but as it were through contact with the sacrifice laid upon it. For holy too is any place where Christ may be.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The consecrated priests must stay in the tent seven days, a sign of staying steadfast in holiness, always near God and keeping his charges.
comments.comment: The law does not allow those who have been enriched with a holy and chosen lot, and have now been consecrated for the priesthood, to go anywhere outside the holy tent (Leviticus 8:33). It bids them sit within until the seventh day (Leviticus 8:35), and all but nails them to the doors, so that they do not cross the threshold. In this, I think, it makes their sitting in holy places a symbol of steadfastness and of remaining in holiness. For we who have been appointed to wait upon God must be firmly set and unshaken in virtue, not straying outside the fitting way nor running away from the mind that befits a priest, but always near God and, as it were, dwelling with him, as was said through the voice of a prophet: ‘Seek earnestly, and dwell with me’ (Isaiah 21:12). Moses ordered this to be done for seven days; the seven signifies that we must be eager to wait upon God at every season, for in a way it means ‘throughout’ and ‘always’. While they are inside the tent, he commands them to keep the charges of the Lord (Leviticus 8:35), hinting that obedience is the fruit of waiting upon God, together with the will to do whatever he may choose to command. This is how we must wait upon the Master of all, since carelessness about what is good always ends in the very last of evils. That is why, as I believe, Moses added, ‘so that you do not die’ (Leviticus 8:35).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the priests stay at the door for seven days.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The eighth day, the day of the resurrection, is the time of Christ's priesthood, when the things of Moses end and the glory of the Lord is seen.
comments.comment: For the time of Christ's priesthood may rightly be understood as the time after the law, that is, the eighth day, on which the resurrection took place, and which is, as it were, the beginning of a new age. For in Christ there is a new creation, as it is written (2 Corinthians 5:17). Once Christ has been revealed on the eighth day, the things of Moses come to an end, for we no longer worship in types and shadows (Hebrews 8:5). Yet the teaching of the law has not fallen silent, for the law is spiritual to those who are spiritual (Romans 7:14), and it always speaks of the mystery of Christ. Moses, then, promised that on the eighth day the glory of the Lord would be seen (Leviticus 9:1–6), for the law announced beforehand the time of our Savior's coming.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Aaron offers first for himself and then for the people, since those chosen for the priesthood must themselves be holy and consecrated.
comments.comment: Again he gives a further command: Aaron is first to offer sacrifices for himself, and after this those for the whole people (Leviticus 9:7). In this, I think, he already makes the matter in some way a type for those of our own day, and indicates very well and clearly that it is right and fitting for those chosen for the priesthood, and for those who receive sanctification in faith, to be holy and consecrated.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Aaron offers first for himself and then for the people.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The sacrifice for Aaron and the people points to the saints' consecration, who die to the world and are made fragrant to God in Christ, who was burned like the calf and the ram.
comments.comment: For my part, I think that the sacrifice for Aaron and for the people neatly hints at the consecration of the saints to God. Emmanuel has now been revealed and has made plain all that concerns him; through him we have been called to sanctification, made acceptable and consecrated, and dedicated to the Father for a fragrant aroma. For notice that, through the rites just described, the perfecting of the priests was carried out according to the law, while it was through him, in turn, that they were sanctified in many ways. For he was burned like a calf outside the camp for sin (Leviticus 9:11); he was offered up in smoke like a ram duly burned whole, all of him, limb by limb, as though for each one and for all (Leviticus 9:13); and he sanctified them by anointing them with blood, as the ram of salvation. Now that the eighth day has dawned, that is, the day on which the glory of Christ became more manifest, when death was abolished and corruption trampled down, priests and people alike bear fruit for God. They do not honor him with things foreign to them, nor delight the Master of all with things from outside, as Israel according to the flesh did (1 Corinthians 10:18), but they show themselves to be a fragrant sacrifice. For in a way, as if in the likeness of the victims, we offer up our own souls in sacrifice and bring them to God. We die to the world and to minding the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5), we endure the putting to death of the passions, and we are all but crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:19–20), so that, passing over to a holy and blameless life, we may live as he wills. The inspired Paul, too, writes something of this kind: ‘Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our body’ (2 Corinthians 4:10). And again: ‘If we endure, we shall also reign with him’ (2 Timothy 2:12). If we are conformed to his death and his sufferings, as it is written, we shall share in the resurrection and the glory as well (Philippians 3:10–11). So then Christ suffered for us outside the gate, as the blessed Paul says, and we too go out of the gate, bearing his reproach (Hebrews 13:12–13); slain in the same way, like a young calf, and burned whole like a ram, we make our life in Christ fragrant to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The people's offering is a goat and the priests' a calf because what belongs to the priests stands higher, and the other victims hint at the virtues of the consecrated.
comments.comment: For the people, a male goat is the sin offering (Leviticus 9:15). And why is that, when a young calf was offered for the cleansing of the priests? Everything that belongs to the priests stands higher: the bringing of sacrifices and the rites of cleansing and purification. And a young calf is larger in body than a goat, and so displays a clear token of the spiritual pre-eminence found in the realities themselves. The young calf and the lamb for the whole burnt offering (Leviticus 9:3) hint at the infancy in Christ of those consecrated in faith. The calf and the ram signify very well endurance and courage, and fruitfulness in gentleness: the calf is the type of the first, the ram of the second (Leviticus 9:4). The fine flour soaked with oil (Leviticus 9:4) shows very clearly the bright hope of the life in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Aaron's lifting of his hands in blessing is the first laying on of hands on the people, a sign of the Spirit coming down upon us.
comments.comment: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed the people (Leviticus 9:22). And see again: here, through Aaron, is as it were the first laying on of hands upon the people. For the true Aaron blesses everyone, priests and people, the small together with the great, as it is written (Psalm 115:13), all but laying his hands on them as well; and the laying on of the hand would be a clear sign of the all-holy Spirit coming down upon us. Before Aaron's priestly service there was no laying on of hands. ‘For the Spirit was not yet,’ as John says, ‘because Jesus was not yet glorified’ (John 7:39).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Aaron's raised hands of blessing point to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The glory of the Lord seen on the eighth day is the Son made manifest, who is slain for us like the calf and is himself the ram, the sacrifice of salvation and the fine flour.
comments.comment: In truth the glory of the Lord was seen on the eighth day; that is, the Son, the glory of God the Father, became manifest. For God named him so when he said to the most holy Moses, ‘As I live, says the Lord, all the earth shall surely be filled with the glory of the Lord’ (Numbers 14:21). It is he himself who makes us consecrated. He is slain for us, like the calf; he sets us free from sin, releases us from every charge, and scours away the filth that comes from being condemned. He likewise, like the ram, is made perfect for a pleasing spiritual aroma; he himself becomes the sacrifice of salvation and sanctifies us with his own blood (Hebrews 13:12); he himself is the fine flour moistened with oil, in the gladness of a holy life, presenting himself for us to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The fire that came down and consumed the sacrifices shows that God welcomes the saints' fruits, and now touches the spiritual sacrifice in the Holy Spirit and not in fire.
comments.comment: … the glory of Christ will shine out purely and clearly, welcoming most gladly the fruits the saints bring, just as then, too, God came down visibly in the form of fire and consumed the sacrifices (Leviticus 9:24). He all but counts the approved life of those sanctified in faith as his food and delight. The passage also hints at a mystery. For then God sent the blaze of fire down upon the divided pieces, as though in some way touching what lay before him, for the Godhead always takes on the guise of fire. But now, when the spiritual sacrifice is set before him, he touches what lies before him in a spiritual way, not in the form of fire but in the Holy Spirit, and makes it life-giving for those who desire to partake of it; and we have received this by faith as true.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Priests must shake off the drunkenness of worldly care, keep away from what is profane, and be able to teach that the law speaks the mystery of Christ.
comments.comment:
But those who have been chosen, on whom the best verdict has fallen, must keep away both from profane company and from worldly care. Through such care even a steady mind may become drunk, and all but be toppled into improper pleasures. …

See, then, that they must keep awake. To handle the sacred liturgy with a darkened mind, and with an anxious heart that is drunk with worldly things, brings death; for some are drunk without wine. For at times the mind, unable to walk upright, slips away toward what is unseemly; the sacred things fall into disarray, and what is performed is no longer in good order but is thrown, as it were, off the straight road. Those who suffer this cannot help but offend God and endure bitter penalties for their carelessness. So one must keep awake and shake off the drunkenness that comes from worldly care. The Savior himself also urges this when he says: ‘Take care that your hearts are not weighed down by anxiety and the cares of this life’ (Luke 21:34).

What our way of sobriety would be, and how we shall remain unprofaned and clean and free of punishment, he indicated at once. For ‘distinguish,’ He says, ‘between holy and profane, and between clean and unclean; and you shall teach the sons of Israel all the statutes that the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses’ (Leviticus 10:10–11). This plainly means that the priests, having shaken off drunkenness, ought to keep away from men who are not holy but profane and unclean. And I think a man would do this very easily if he is himself unprofaned and clean; for ‘every living creature,’ it says, ‘loves its like, and a man will cling to one like himself’ (Sirach 13:15–16).

Besides this, they ought to be wise and able to teach; for whoever has charge of the rational flock must be sober and able to teach (1 Timothy 3:2).
