He puts it very well when he says, ‘You shall teach,’ that is, ‘You shall make plain,’ so that the hearers may be able to see that the law is a tutor (Galatians 3:24) and speaks the mystery of Christ. For nothing in it is hard to grasp or needs teaching, unless it is understood spiritually; for the historical account is entirely simple and free of the shadows of obscurity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the priests must not drink when they serve and must distinguish and teach.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Scripture names many beasts as unclean or clean so that those who serve God may know what conduct would keep them from acceptance and what leaves them blameless.
comments.comment: Observe, then, that Scripture, bringing forward to good purpose countless kinds of beasts, and of birds and swimming creatures too, brands some as unclean and wholly defiled, and accepts others again and clears them of reproach, so that those who serve God may rightly know what conduct would keep them from being accepted, and by wisely abstaining from what they will be far from blame and will shine, worthy of acceptance and honored by the verdict from above.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The parted hoof is the one who walks rightly both toward himself and toward others, and the cud-chewing is the man who always turns over and grinds fine the doctrines of God.
comments.comment: The law, then, always likens such a person, in a way, to a parted hoof, that is, to a foot divided in two (Leviticus 11:3). For the foot would always be for us a symbol and type of the road we travel in practical action. Indeed we speak of those who are truly eager to go blamelessly toward what leads to their good as walking with a straight foot. David also sings somewhere: ‘For my foot has stood on level ground’ (Psalm 26:12), that is, I have walked in righteousness and uprightness, and I have hated what is crooked. And of those who love sin he says: ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in their paths’ (Romans 3:15–16). So the foot is a symbol of the road we travel in deeds. And the parting of the hoof would be a clear type of our being able to walk rightly and beyond reproach in both ways: in what concerns ourselves, and also toward others. … Suppose, then, there is someone who knows how to walk rightly and skillfully in both ways, and is able to benefit both himself and others (I mean by the quality of his character). Suppose that besides this he is sensible and very wise, and gives his heart to the words about God as a kind of lodging and dwelling place; that he is always turning over within himself, this way and that, the meanings of the divine doctrines, and so knows how to search them out often and wisely, grinding fine, as it were, the thoughts he has come to know so exactly. Such a person will surely resemble an animal that brings up the cud: it is always bringing back up the food in its belly and putting it under its teeth, so that it may be ground finer still and, made fine enough to digest, may turn to its benefit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the parted hoof and the chewing of the cud stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The split hoof teaches us to travel by both word and deed, and if one must stand alone, let it be deed, since an unbridled word has often pushed people over cliffs.
comments.comment:
That is also why Moses’ law accepts the split hoof: that through riddles it may teach us to journey by both — by word and by deed. I think the split hoof in the law signifies this: that we journey by word and deed, neither acting without reason nor holding a word apart from deed.

If something from such things wants to stand alone, let it be deed and not word. An unbridled word has often pushed those who have it over cliffs; deed never has (Leviticus 11:3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Matthew

comments.capsule: The law does not make any creature profane but takes the natural traits of each animal as pictures of human character, as we ourselves call the bold lions and the gentle sheep.
comments.comment:
It is quite clear, then, that the law by no means makes anything that exists profane, but knows that all things are pure to the pure (Titus 1:15). Rather, by taking the natural traits of each animal very aptly as pictures of the qualities of human character, it does no small good. And you could learn from the following, too, that what I say is true and beyond doubt. For he is seen to command that things condemned by everyone must be abhorred: I mean the camel and the rock badger, the night raven and the cormorant, the gecko and the shrew, and things still more shameful than these (Leviticus 11:4–5; Leviticus 11:17; Leviticus 11:30). Would not the lawgiver’s aim be plain, then, at least in these cases, my good friend?

Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: So we must aptly carry over to the quality of character the traits that are naturally present in certain irrational animals, each animal, so to speak, depicting in itself the ways of a certain kind of person and indicating what traits he has. For are we not ourselves accustomed, in a way, to call those who are very hot-blooded and very strong, and who surpass others in boldness, boars or lions or something else of that kind; and to call those who are gentle and quiet, and whose minds are humble, sheep and doves, and sometimes to crown them with the name ‘calm’, giving to each person’s ways the fitting description drawn from things more easily seen?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the aim of the food laws: the animals are pictures of human character.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The camel, the largest beast, and the hare and rock badger, the smallest, stand for great and small alike, since with God there is no partiality and unclean works condemn both.
comments.comment: As an example of the animal that does not part the hoof yet brings up the cud, then, the law takes the camel, a strong and very large beast, and the hare and the rock badger, which look smaller, one might say, than all the others (Leviticus 11:4–6). In this way, I think, it took in everything at once by means of the extremes, and left out nothing that lies between them. It is as though one were to say: ‘From the very high and the highest of all, down to the small and the very lowest, everyone who is like this is loathsome and unclean.’ For there is no partiality with God, as it is written (Romans 2:11). If someone is great and proud, raised high by wealth and worldly glory, he will receive a verdict without honor or reward if he is liable to the charges of wickedness. And if someone is small, living with poverty and obscurity, he will be condemned as unclean unless he can boast of a virtuous way of life. Nor could anyone turn his lowliness into a pretext for claiming that the just Judge must have mercy on him, if he lacks what is fitting in deeds, that is, in deeds of godliness and virtue. So the camel, the hare and the rock badger would be a clear type of small and great alike.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the camel, hare and rock badger are named together.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The animals that fail in either mark show the person who has good works without right doctrine or doctrine without good works, who is incomplete in virtue and unclean.
comments.comment: So the law has shown in a riddle the person who is excellent and fully formed in virtue, as in an animal that by nature parts the hoof and brings up the cud. And it teaches in turn that it is good and profitable to make a habit of shaking off the person who is not of this mind, who limps, as it were, toward the good and falls behind in the perfection of virtue. It does this by giving its favorable verdict neither to the animals that bring up the cud without having the parted hoof, nor to those that part the hoof by nature if they do not chew the cud; rather, it records their uncleanness and numbers them among the things that defile (Leviticus 11:4–8). … Then the one who prides himself on good works but falls short of right doctrine, and does not hold the words of truth in his mind, would rightly be thought incomplete in virtue, and he stands far from deserving admiration. And it is plain that the reverse is also true. For right doctrine and a sweet concern for the divine words would profit us nothing toward being held perfect in virtue if brightness in deeds were not yoked with them. The one who is skilled in both will carry off the verdict of full approval; but for the one who lacks either, whatever admiration he wins for goodness will have no strength. The Savior also points to something of this kind when he says that the one who teaches but does not also do is called least in the kingdom of heaven, while the one who has done and taught is great and distinguished (Matthew 5:19). Under the law, then, the one who falls short in either of the two is unclean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The pig shows that boasting in works is useless without the word that accords with godliness, just as faith is dead without works.
comments.comment: The law also brings forward the pig as unclean, because it parts the hoof but is not made by nature to chew its food again, that is, to bring up the cud (Leviticus 11:7). In this way it shows that boasting in works is feeble and useless without the word that accords with godliness. For just as faith without works is dead (James 2:26), so the reverse is also true: good order of life and decency in deeds are surely dead when the knowledge of God is absent and the word of godliness has not made its home in our souls. This good order stays low; it is bent toward the earth, and seems somehow afraid to lift its eye upward. We shall find not a few who have suffered something of this kind. At times they lead a dignified and pure life, but because they have not come to know the One who is God by nature and in truth, they fix the eye of their mind, as it were, on earthly things alone. Such a person, too, is unclean; for ‘no one is crowned unless he competes according to the rules,’ as it is written (2 Timothy 2:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the pig is unclean though it parts the hoof.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The Jews' pride is that they know why swine are unclean, and these distinctions were symbols of realities until Jesus came and cleansed all foods.
comments.comment: Nor do the Jews take pride in abstaining from swine as if it were some great thing. Their pride is rather that, having learned the nature of clean and unclean animals, they know the reason for the distinction and that the swine is ranked among the unclean (Leviticus 11:7). These things, too, were symbols of certain realities until the coming of Jesus. After Him it was said to His disciple, who did not yet understand the meaning of these things and said, “Nothing common or unclean has entered my mouth” (Acts 11:8), “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10:15).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book V

comments.capsule: We are not to eat the flesh or touch the carcasses of the unclean, which means keeping away from such people in life and from their writings after death.
comments.comment: And that we ought to keep away from such people and in no way be seen to have any share with them, the law made clear by saying: ‘You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses’ (Leviticus 11:8). That is, it means that you shall not keep company with them while they live. And if one of them should happen to die, you will keep your own mind undefiled, not so much as touching, so to speak, the things they have produced, that is, their discourses and their foul writings; for such things are the remains of a person’s life. Yet handling such remains is just what the untaught heretics are in the habit of doing. For those who became the leaders of the ignorance that is in them have, beyond dispute, gone astray, and they have left with their own disciples what amount to the remains of their own impiety. These disciples welcome them with great delight and take them to live in their minds, and so they carry a stain that is hard to wash off, as though they were handling the flesh of carcasses, which is full of the worst stench and uncleanness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Fish with fins and scales swim up toward the light and slip through nets, while shellfish creep in the mud and are easily caught.
comments.comment: Those creatures in the waters that the Creator of all has fashioned well after the pattern of fishes are always rowing their way along, as it were, by thrusting out their fins, and they move strongly and very swiftly wherever they may choose. When the sun sends the warm stroke of its rays down into the waters from above, they swim upward and all but dare to leap out of the water itself, refusing to stay below always; and they easily slip through the nets of those who hunt them. But those that are not furnished with scales and fins (those, that is, that live in hard casings and are clothed in a shell that grows with them) know almost nothing of what is above. They are always creeping down into the weeds at the bottom, and they love to linger in muddy places. They are sluggish and easily caught, and anyone who has once caught sight of them can take them without the least effort. That is the plain and true account of those creatures.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The eagle, vulture and similar birds picture the boaster with a lifted-up mind, and the kite and raven the plunderers clever at wrongdoing.
comments.comment: The law, then, rejects the eagle, the bearded vulture, the sea eagle, and the vulture as well. For birds like these fly about on high; they love to pride themselves on the loftiest heights, and they hate what is low. ‘The young of the vulture,’ it says, ‘fly to the heights’ (Job 5:7). Such, in a way, is the boaster, the man of overweening haughtiness, who has his mind lifted up within himself, who is used to looking down on a gentle and moderate frame of mind, and who has no love at all for associating with the lowly (Romans 12:16). Together with these the law also condemns the kite and its kind, and the raven and its kind. By these it signifies very well the kind of people who know how to plunder and are clever at wrongdoing: the kite is a type of the first, and the deep, jet-black raven of the second.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Moses understood the natures of animals and the demons akin to them, and called unclean those the Egyptians reckoned prophetic, as the wolf, the fox, the eagle and the hawk, which Scripture never names for anything good.
comments.comment:
Hence, if I have admired anything else in Moses, I will declare this too worthy of admiration. He understood the different natures of animals, and, whether he learned from God about them and about the demons akin to each animal, or found it out himself as he rose by wisdom, in his ordinance concerning animals he said that all those reckoned prophetic by the Egyptians and the rest of mankind are unclean, and that, in general, those not of this kind are clean (Leviticus 11:1–47; Deuteronomy 14:3–20). Among the unclean in Moses are the wolf, the fox and the serpent, the eagle, the hawk and the like (Leviticus 11:13–19, 27, 42; Deuteronomy 14:12–18). And, in general, not only in the Law but also in the Prophets you would find these animals taken as examples of the very worst things, and you would never find a wolf or a fox named in connection with anything good.

It seems, then, that there is a certain fellowship between each kind of demon and each kind of animal. And just as among men some are stronger than others, not necessarily because of their character, in the same way some demons may be more powerful than others in morally indifferent matters. Some of them use these animals to deceive men, according to the will of the one who in our teaching is called “the ruler of this age” (John 12:31; 1 Corinthians 2:6), while others give their forewarnings through another kind. And see how foul the demons are, so that even weasels are used by some to reveal the future.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book IV

comments.capsule: The ostrich, hawk and similar birds picture those who prey on others without love, and the owl and bat the lovers of night who hate the light of Christ.
comments.comment: … ‘And the ostrich and the gull’ (Leviticus 11:16). For these, I think, are most insatiable, always gathering up whatever comes their way. Then it says: ‘And the hawk and its kind, the night raven, the cormorant, the ibis, the purple gallinule, the pelican and the swan’ (Leviticus 11:16–18). These too would portray in themselves those who plot cruelly and savagely against others and fasten without restraint on whomever they can, so that they do not shrink even from putting some in danger and fear for their very lives. For the hawk swoops fiercely on every weaker bird; it darts at sparrows, and when it catches them it kills them. The cormorant, the ibis and the purple gallinule, and I would add the pelican too, fall furiously on the fish and make their destruction their food. Such, as far as conduct and savagery of character go, are all who count it as nothing to destroy others for the sake of their own pleasure. They have thrust aside the law of mutual love and offended against the ordinances of love, and it would be altogether fitting for them to hear this, even from us: ‘Do not seek your own interests, but also those of others (Philippians 2:4; 1 Corinthians 10:24); for love,’ it says, ‘does no wrong to a neighbor’ (Romans 13:10). Again, it said that one must refuse the owl, the heron, the plover and their kind, the hoopoe and the bat (Leviticus 11:16–19). These, I think, are lovers of the night. They delight in the darkness and are practiced at taking their flight in it as their sweetest pleasure, but they hate the light of the sun and cannot bear to do anything in it. Such birds would plainly stand for those who work evil. For what Christ said is true: ‘Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, that they have been done in God’ (John 3:20–21).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The law names small winged creatures as unclean as well as the eagle, treating small and great alike as unclean if they work outrageous deeds.
comments.comment: The winged creeping things too are unclean, those ‘which go,’ it says, ‘on all fours’ (Leviticus 11:20): for example, the various kinds of flies and anything akin to them. These are countless, small and loathsome, and they cannot fly high. We must therefore look closely at the reason why the law came down even to these. For just as, when it made mention of the beasts, it named the camel and then added the hare (Leviticus 11:4–6), declaring all those charged with wickedness equally unclean, whether one were great or small — for, as it is written, there is no partiality with God (Romans 2:11) — so here too it calls to mind the eagle, naming the most kingly of birds, but then comes down again to the very smallest of winged creatures, putting small and great on an equal footing if one is a worker of outrageous deeds, and so cannot escape the condemnation that is his due.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Locusts, which leap up, picture the worldly person who is not bound to earthly things and sets his mind at times on things above.
comments.comment: [The law sets apart] … the locust and the young locust and creatures like them (Leviticus 11:21–22), because of their strength: they can leap up, they are least inclined to linger below, and they often rise on high and spring easily from place to place. Such, in a way, is the person who lives a worldly life and yet is not wholly without a share of decency in other respects and of love for God. Such a person is not bound altogether to earthly things, nor does he settle among what is below. He has learned in some measure to set his mind on the things above (Colossians 3:2), and at times he wins approval, springing up toward the things above and flying over the things of earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Washing the garment and being clean toward evening point to Christ's mystery, when we were cleansed through baptism near the end of the age.
comments.comment: As for one who touches unclean things and has been defiled, he must wash his garment, and toward evening, the law says, he will be clean (Leviticus 11:24–25). In this it very aptly points to the mystery of Christ, through whom we have been cleansed and are rich in the forgiveness that comes through holy baptism. This came about, clearly, at the time of his coming, a time that fell, as it were, toward evening, that is, when the present age was already drawing toward its end. Or do we not say that the Word of God became man in the last times?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The wild beasts picture savage robbers, and the mouse, weasel and lizard picture cowardly thieves who prowl by night.
comments.comment: Through the wild beasts the law seems to point to the most savage of robbers, who count as nothing even murder, the evil beyond all others, and who all but devour whomever they come upon, destroying without pity, with all mercy cast out. Through the mouse and the weasel, and the creatures close to them and like them (I mean the land crocodile, the lizard and the gecko), it points to the easily startled and cowardly kinds of thieves who prowl about at night.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Everything of the robber's kind is unclean and defiles those who touch it, and the law spared springs and cisterns so that its rule might not be impossible to keep.
comments.comment: So everything of the robber’s kind is unclean, whether a man has a beast’s ways and bloodthirsty hands, or whether he pilfers small things, like the mouse and the weasel, and, after the manner of the mole and the gecko, springs up walls and onto roofs. And if anyone touches those so defiled, he will share in their guilt, for fellowship with such people makes those who share it wholly and altogether unclean. The defiled vessels would stand as a type of human beings, for man has the form of a vessel. Yet the law frees a spring of water, a cistern and a gathering of water from having to be defiled, even if something defiled under the law should happen to fall into them. In this, I think, it does not let those under the law consider the matter altogether burdensome and hard to carry through, or find the keeping of the law impossible to practice, as they would if they suffered harm here, in their most vital needs. For at times they would have had to leave their cities and houses, since their water would have been defiled and they would have lost a use they needed and could not do without. So the law relaxed the strictness of its literal rule for the sake of what was necessary and useful for those under the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Even the carcass of a clean animal defiles, as a brother who is defiled by dead works defiles whoever clings to him, and he is cleansed by water toward evening.
comments.comment: Yet it says that even the carcass of a clean animal is unclean, just as the others are, and it added that this too will defile whoever touches it. … This, I think, is plainly the same as the saying: ‘If anyone who bears the name of brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or a reviler, or a robber, do not even eat with such a one’ (1 Corinthians 5:11). For if anyone at all who is held in esteem for holiness, who has already been cleansed and received through faith into spiritual fellowship, undergoes the deadness that comes from sin, ‘let him be loathsome,’ it says, ‘and hated.’ For, defiled by dead works, he surely defiles whoever clings to him. But if anyone does suffer that defilement, let him become clean through water toward evening; and what this means, our argument has already shown us plainly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The law used these creatures to shape character, since no dead animal or food can defile the soul, so we must keep away even from the company of the wicked.
comments.comment: For I think we must soberly keep away not only from doing the same deeds as the wicked, but even from merely keeping company with them. ‘For whoever touches pitch will be defiled,’ it says (Sirach 13:1). And the saying is true. That the law took up the lessons of these examples for the forming of character, one may learn from what follows. For it said again: ‘You shall not make your souls loathsome with any of the creeping things that creep on the earth, and you shall not be defiled by them, and you shall not be unclean through them; for I am the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 11:43–44). For what defilement could an animal’s dying, or touching what has died, bring upon the human soul? What harm could food do, which goes into the belly and is sent out into the drain, as the Savior said (Matthew 15:17)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be defiled by creeping things, since no animal or food can defile the soul.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The law's words 'if any woman conceives seed' exempt the Virgin, who conceived by the Holy Spirit, and the unclean woman who bears is human nature, subject to corruption since the transgression.
comments.comment: For although the law proceeds against every woman who bears a male or a female child, and makes its denunciation of us as general as can be, the holy Virgin, from whom we say Christ according to the flesh was born, is exempted from the reproach. Look, if you will, at the precision of the law. For it says ‘a woman,’ and perhaps not all women without distinction, but ‘if any woman conceives seed and bears a male child,’ let her be unclean (Leviticus 12:2). But the divine body was formed from the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:20), fashioned in the holy Virgin in a way beyond words, and paying little heed to the laws of nature. For the firstborn of the saints, the firstfruits of those who have received rebirth from God through the Spirit, had no need at all of the sowing of seed. Of these it is plainly said: ‘who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God’ (John 1:13). So the holy Virgin escaped the law’s accusation, for she in no way conceived from seed, but brought forth the divine Child by the working of the Holy Spirit. But the woman who gives birth and is unclean for that reason would be, in all likelihood and by a sound reading, human nature. For the present we shall give nature the role of the woman. Nature is accused by the law and called liable to defilements because it gives birth into corruption, and because it is no longer in the state in which it first received its being from God, for it was made for incorruption (Wisdom of Solomon 2:23), but has rather been carried off course into the necessity of being corrupted. It was condemned for the transgression, and nature has endured, against nature, the penalty that came from the divine curse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The phrase 'if she is inseminated' may have been set down so that Mary, who bore a male child without being inseminated, would not be thought unclean.
comments.comment: “A woman who, if she is inseminated, bears a male child” (Leviticus 12:2). The phrase “if she is inseminated,” placed before “and bears a male child,” will seem to be redundant. But I am considering whether perhaps it was said for this reason: so that prophetically Mary, having borne a male child not from being inseminated, might not be thought unclean after giving birth to the Savior. Even without the phrase “if she is inseminated” being set down, Mary could be understood not to be unclean, for she was not simply a woman, but a virgin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse has the seemingly redundant words 'if she is inseminated'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Leviticus

comments.capsule: The mother is unclean seven plus thirty-three days for a son and double for a daughter, according to those learned in these matters, until the child in the womb is formed.
comments.comment:
The law itself, Palladius, which condemns us, has shown us the way. For ‘let her be set apart as unclean,’ it says, ‘for seven days’ (Leviticus 12:2). And let her count another thirty-three, and she shall remain in her unclean blood (Leviticus 12:4); that is, clearly, for a male child. But if she bears a female, it says, the separation is double, and double too the count of the other days (Leviticus 12:5). So if the child born is male, the mother is unclean and in defilement for seven and thirty-three days, that is, forty; but if female, for twice seven and sixty-six, that is, eighty.

Palladius: And what, then, would be the reason for this?

Cyril: Once again the law lifts us from bodily examples to the understanding of what is more hidden, and it paints the things of the senses as a kind of picture of spiritual contemplation. Now those who are learned in these matters say that if what is conceived in the womb is male, it takes on its form only when forty days have passed; but if female, it comes to this more slowly, being weak and feeble. They say that it needs twice forty days, that is, eighty, to be distinctly formed. So the mother of a male child was unclean for forty days; but the mother of a female was in defilements and uncleannesses for a full eighty days, that is, until what is in the womb is exactly formed and has come to human shape.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Mary did not conceive from seed and so needed no purification, and the offering was made for the sake of the whole race.
comments.comment:
But neither did Mary nor the infant need purification rites. For it says: "A woman who has conceived and bears a male shall be unclean for seven days" (Leviticus 12:2). But Mary did not conceive; therefore she did not need purification rites.

"A woman who has conceived and bears a male shall be unclean for seven days" (Leviticus 12:2). Why? Because she has brought another Adam into life. "But if she bears a female, she shall be unclean for twice seven days" (Leviticus 12:5). Why did he assign double the days here? Because Eve is again born from Eve, a woman is born, the fragile vessel, the weak jar, the shattered pot, the rod of deceit, the guide of disobedience, the counselor of the serpent.

But just as you have heard the charges against woman, come now and learn the achievement that came from her. A woman brought virginity into the world. She contained in her womb the God whom creation cannot contain. She bore in the flesh the one who fashioned our race. She was the first to receive Jesus from the dead, the first to begin the proclamation of the rising, the first to announce the joy to the disciples.

"A woman who," it says, "has conceived" (Leviticus 12:2). But the Mother of God was a woman, yet she did not undergo what women undergo. For her womb did not receive a man's seed. The field of Mary saw no plow; the virginal vineyard endured no mattock. So the offering was not for her sake, but for the sake of the whole race.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: Homily I on the Presentation

comments.capsule: On the eighth day, after the time of the law, we are circumcised through the Spirit and are born into life and incorruption through Christ, the spotless lamb.
comments.comment: But since on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), that is, after the time of the law and that ancient Sabbath rest, we have been circumcised through the Spirit with a circumcision not made by hands (Colossians 2:11), and have been formed into Christ, having become sharers in his divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), then we have shaken off the charges against us; the filth too has been wiped away, and all our defilement is gone. For we are no longer born into corruption because of the transgression in Adam, but into life and incorruption because of the justification in Christ (Romans 5:18), who endured slaughter on our behalf as a spotless and true lamb (1 Peter 1:19), as a divine turtledove discerned by the mind (Leviticus 12:6). For in no other way have we been saved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the circumcision on the eighth day as fulfilled in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The prophets teach that a sin offering is made even for the newborn, as not pure from sin.
comments.comment: But the prophets, hinting at some wise teaching about the things of becoming, say that a sacrifice “for sin” is offered even for those just born, as not pure from sin (Leviticus 12:6–8). They also say: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 51:5). And they declare as well that “sinners were estranged from the womb,” and they also say, in a surprising way, “they went astray from the belly, they spoke lies” (Psalm 58:3).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VII

comments.capsule: The law's rules about leprosy cannot rebuke bodily affliction we do not choose, so they must be a type of the diseases of the soul, where wrongdoing makes the rebuke holy.
comments.comment: Now it is clear to anyone, I think, that the law could not reasonably be thought to rebuke us in these matters for what happens by necessity and against our will. For why should a bodily affliction be punished, and how could the one who has fallen into fleshly infirmities justly incur the law’s condemnation? It is wise, then, and necessary to take these bodily conditions as an image and type of the diseases in souls. For in this way the law would be spiritual (Romans 7:14), and what God has declared on each matter at various times would be a holy verdict, not subjecting to penalties those caught by diseases they did not choose, but those in whose case the fact of wrongdoing would make the rebuke holy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the leprosy laws are read as a picture of diseases of the soul.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Leprosy is a deadness that sinks deep and turns the hair white, while the white patch only resembles it, so the law condemns the leper and releases the one with the white patch after testing.
comments.comment: Leprosy is a most grievous disease of human bodies, hard to escape and devouring, and it comes about by a deadening. The sore is hollowed out at once, as the skin is consumed and keeps sinking deeper, since the corruption always creeps downward. That, I think, is why the hair growing on those places withers and turns white, and like a plant it perishes along with the soil beneath it. Such, then, is leprosy. The white patch, on the other hand, is a bodily ailment that resembles leprosy, except that it does not drive the harm deep or send the feeling of the disease into the parts within. It floats, as it were, on the surface and barely blooms on the body. It does not turn the hair white, nor does it spread beyond control; with very few remedies it is easily reined in, and the flesh where it broke out returns to health. So leprosy is an undoubted deadness, while the white patch raises some suspicion of leprosy but is not in truth the same thing, that is, leprosy and deadness. The law therefore condemns the leper as unclean, since he has already suffered deadness; but it acquits of the charge the one sick with the white patch, since he has come under suspicion of leprosy but is not actually leprous. This is why it says that if there is a scar with a mark, and a leprous sore, and the skin looks hollowed, and the hair also changes to white, dying, it may be, together with the flesh beneath it, then it will certainly be leprosy (Leviticus 13:2–3); for the deadness creeps deep. But if there is a white patch with a mark, without any hollowing of the skin and without the hair changing to white, let it be tested, it says, by the priest, and let the man be set apart a second time (Leviticus 13:4–5). For it is not unlikely that the passing of the days itself, putting the ailment to the test, may sometimes show the exact truth to those who examine it. In one case the hair takes on another color as the skin hollows, and the white patch has turned into leprosy. But if none of these things has happened, ‘let him be released,’ it says, ‘from the charge’ (Leviticus 13:6). For the condition is not leprosy, but something that resembles leprosy and comes very close to it, namely the white patch.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The man defiled in soul and mind and full of the world's wickedness is dead and a leper of the mind, unclean in the eyes of Christ.
comments.comment: The one, then, who is defiled in soul and mind, and is full of the world’s wickedness, is dead, held fast in the works of deadness. And if anyone chose to call such a state a leprosy of the mind in the true sense, he would not miss the right word. Such a person, then, is unclean in the eyes of Christ. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall pronounce him unclean’ (Leviticus 13:3). For at the divine judgment seat, counted among those who dearly love sin, he will hear: ‘Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you’ (Matthew 7:23; Luke 13:27; Matthew 25:41).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The white patch pictures those who are still at mere desire and have not yet acted, and while sin lies only in desire the mind has not yet suffered deadness, though it is not free of rebuke.
comments.comment: But to the white patch and the scar with a mark we should liken those who are still at the stage of mere desire and have not yet carried their thought into action. Or do you not agree that it is true that pleasures and thoughts spring up in us ahead of the deeds, and dawn, as it were, before them, calling us toward something the law condemns? … Yet while the sin still lies only in desires, the mind stands between the two and looks toward both. It is free to lean toward whichever it may choose; it has not yet suffered deadness, though it has come very near to the evil and is in labor with the passion. The Savior’s disciple has clearly told us something of this kind: ‘Let no one,’ he says, ‘when he is tempted, say, “I am tempted by God”; for God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is completed, brings forth death’ (James 1:13–15). … So being wholly dead, as in leprosy (I mean the leprosy of the mind) and as in the condition of deadness that comes from sin, would perhaps come about not in desires alone but when they issue in deeds. As long as the evil is still in the mind’s birth pangs, there is not yet deadness and not yet death, for ‘not every sin leads to death,’ as the Savior’s disciple has said (1 John 5:16–17). There is still only a suspicion that it may suffer the things that can bring death. And we said that the white patch looks like leprosy, or comes near to it. ‘The priest shall look,’ it says, at the one held by the condition (I mean the white patch); and if it is seen not to be changing into leprosy, he shall not pronounce him unclean, but rather shall set him apart (Leviticus 13:4–5). For before God it is not beyond rebuke even to dwell in desires and come near to evil. But if the condition, it says, resists the change and has not turned toward the worse, ‘let him be clean’ (Leviticus 13:6).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The washing of the clothes after cleansing foretells holy baptism.
comments.comment: And notice that the law says that the one freed from the charge will be clean once he has washed his clothes (Leviticus 13:6). In this the law foretells the cleansing through water, and, as in types that the bodily senses can perceive, it sketches for us the mystery of holy baptism.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Leprosy covering the whole body pictures one who has died wholly to sin and is clean, but any living flesh left makes him unclean, so nothing dead must be in us if we live for God and nothing of sin alive if we have died to sin.
comments.comment: For we must put to death our members that are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire and covetousness (Colossians 3:5), and so seem in some way already to have died to sin, and that completely, no longer living in it. The divine Paul will assure us of this when he says: ‘What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? By no means! How shall we who died to sin still live in it?’ (Romans 6:1–2). So then, just as in the case of one who has chosen to live for Christ the law made being partly dead liable to its penalties, so too in the case of one who has died to sin, to live in it would again be a defilement, and one not free of the charge the law brings. For this reason it says that if leprosy should cover the whole body, a kind of deadness spreading over every member, it would signify the one who has died to sin; and there is no longer defilement in the body (Leviticus 13:12–13). For he is clean, it says, who has died to sin wholly and utterly, who has given it no place, and has not, as it were, let it lodge within him. ‘But if,’ it says, ‘living flesh should again be seen in him, the living flesh will defile him’ (Leviticus 13:14–15). For to live for sin at all, even in part, makes the sick man abominable. ‘For a little leaven,’ it says, ‘leavens the whole lump’ (1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9), and the saying is true. But if, it says, the living flesh should be restored and change back to leprosy, let the charges be dropped: he is clean (Leviticus 13:16–17). For he has been freed even from still living partly for sin, since his mind has moved over to the deadness that is praised and has made a truly excellent change. So then, to sum up what I have said: if we live for God, let nothing be dead in us; if we have died to sin, let nothing of sin be alive in us. For this is the bright road for us of a way of life fit for saints, one with nothing in it open to reproach.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: We please God either by living for Christ and refusing the deadness of sin, or by dying to sin and refusing to live in it, and so complete leprosy and partial leprosy are judged differently.
comments.comment: In two ways, I think, we shall achieve the life that is most lawful in the sight of God, who loves virtue. Either, living for him, we refuse the deadness that comes from passions and sin, and this is not to suffer leprosy; for a partial deadness befalling a living body is what makes leprosy. Or, in the other way, through a good deadness, and by no longer consenting to live in a worldly way, we shall bind on, like a crown, the vote of approval awarded to all that is best. For the inspired Paul writes thus to some: ‘So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 6:11). Living in Christ, then, by striving to accomplish what pleases him, we shall hate being put to death, plainly, by passions and sins; and having died to sin, as it is written (Romans 6:2), we shall thrust away living in it, because we think rightly. … So we live for Christ when we order our lives by the Gospel and loathe the deadness that comes from sin, that is, the death that comes from the passions. Indeed the inspired Peter writes of Christ: ‘He bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness’ (1 Peter 2:24). For I think that those who care to live a shining life must go far from everything that can bring death, and must succeed in ridding themselves of defilements.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: If the passion has gone no further than thoughts the man is set apart and not cast out, but if it breaks into deeds he is liable again, so we must not reopen wounds already healed.
comments.comment: … For if the disease has gone no further, it says, than thoughts alone, the one who suffers it is by no means free of rebuke, for he will be set apart (Leviticus 13:21); yet he is not cast out entirely, nor is he wholly dead. But if the passion should shoot through the thoughts and through desire itself, having already undergone in some way a complete change for the worse, it will make the one who has fallen sick again liable to the penalties for defilement (Leviticus 13:22). So we must guard above all against waking passions that have already been lulled to sleep, against reopening the wounds of the mind, and against running back to where we were at the beginning. Otherwise we too shall hear a saint crying aloud: ‘What the true proverb says has happened to them: The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing, to wallowing in the mire’ (2 Peter 2:22).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The head and the beard, types of the mind and of wise understanding, show the sickness of the mind, which Christ examines closely.
comments.comment: Defilement in us is twofold, Palladius: of the flesh and of the spirit (2 Corinthians 7:1). The flesh is stained by its own outrageous and unholy passions; the soul and the mind are stained above all by straying from right doctrine to worse things and by the corruption of sound faith, and besides these by tricks and deceits, false oaths, gossip, conceit, quarrels, jealousies (2 Corinthians 12:20), and whatever lies near these and is akin to them and stands equally accused of wickedness. So in these things the law seems perhaps to be calling to mind the passions of the soul, and to wish to point out the sicknesses that usually arise in the mind. For the head is a type of the mind, and the beard a type of wise understanding, since the beard too is a sign of maturity. So the High Priest of all, that is, Christ, watches over our affairs and examines them closely; he will look into the mind itself and test the inward and hidden heart.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: A mind only at the start of its sickness is set apart and rebuked but not cast out, and the shaving shows that all lies bare before the eyes of God.
comments.comment: But if the mind is, as it were, at the beginning of its sickness, yet is not seen to have turned aside entirely into the sickness I spoke of, he is set apart and made subject to measured rebukes, but he will not be wholly unclean, nor estranged from God; when he has washed his garments he will be clean (Leviticus 13:34), that is, he will receive as his help the justification that is in Christ. And the shaving of the hair, which lays the wound bare before the priest, would signify that everything, as it were, is cleared out of the way, and that whatever he may wish to look upon lies bare and unhindered before the eyes of the Godhead. ‘For there is no creature hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes,’ as it is written (Hebrews 4:13).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The white rash is a sickness but not a deadly one, like our faults, which the Judge forgives out of love for humankind because he knows how we were formed.
comments.comment: For our nature suffers from weakness and from slipping easily into wrongdoing; and ‘No one is clean from filth,’ as Holy Scripture says, ‘not even if his life on earth were a single day’ (Job 14:4–5). This is why the divine David sings to us: ‘If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand? For with you is propitiation’ (Psalm 130:3–4). See, then, how the law kindly drops the charge against us for faults like these, and in its gentleness cleanses those who, through human slipping, have fallen into lapses that are bitter and all but involuntary. … And yet, if one looks into the matter strictly, to have a white rash would be a disease of the flesh and close to leprosy. But it does not suffer deadness, nor is it past all hope. Our faults are something like this: they are admittedly sicknesses, but not to the point of death and the ruin of the soul. The Judge does not examine too strictly, because ‘he knows how we were formed’ (Psalm 103:14), and he was not unaware of the weakness of our nature. So he grants forgiveness out of his innate love for humankind. And this, I think, is what is meant by ‘A white rash is clean’ (Leviticus 13:39).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the white rash is declared clean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Hair loss, a condition of the head which types the mind, shows small and involuntary faults that the law pardons, since freedom from all passion belongs to the age to come.
comments.comment:
So the law sketches these too, again in a figure, and says this: ‘If anyone’s head loses its hair, he is bald; he is clean. And if his head loses its hair at the front, he is bald on the forehead; he is clean’ (Leviticus 13:40–41). The involuntary loss of hair would be a condition of the head; and we were saying just now that the head is named as a type of the mind, for the head is the dwelling place of the mind, at least in the opinion of some.

Palladius: I will remember.

Cyril: So the conditions of the bodily head would fittingly show the sicknesses of the mind, small ones again, and of the kind it is right to pardon. Therefore the law releases us from every human passion and from the involuntary defilements that may befall us, since our nature cannot help suffering weakness; and to be wholly freed from passions does not belong to the present time, but would befit the age to come, when sin will be shaken from its foundations and we shall pass over into a life wholly free from harm.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Even small passions, such as a little anger, defile when they are left to grow into worse things, as leprosy on a bald head shows.
comments.comment: For sometimes even small passions run on until they carry the weight of offenses, and they defile terribly when we do not cut them short and they have gained, as it were, an open passage toward worse things, one wholly unrebuked. I mean something like this: someone is sometimes a little angry, and the passion has taken hold in him, as happens to a human being. Let it be cut short by gentle means, so that the small fault may not grow until, little by little, a charge that leads to death is found against those who suffer it. This is what is meant when leprosy happens to break out on a bald head: the slide from nothing toward worse things, taking place, as it were, in a type. So I say that this was rightly spoken by blessed David: ‘Be angry, and do not sin’ (Psalm 4:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what leprosy breaking out on a bald head stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The leper's head is uncovered and his garments loosened so that he may be recognized and others may not share his uncleanness, as the Apostle says of sinners.
comments.comment: “And the leper in whom is the plague of leprosy—his garments shall be loosened, and his head uncovered” (Leviticus 13:45). Why does it command that the leper’s head be uncovered and his garments loosened? So that he may be recognizable, and those who approach may not share in his uncleanness. Thus the Apostle said about sinners: “Keep yourselves away from every brother walking disorderly and not according to the tradition which you received from us” (2 Thessalonians 3:6), and, “If anyone named a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a drunkard, or a reviler, or a robber—do not eat with such a person” (1 Corinthians 5:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the leper's head and garments are marked.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Leviticus

comments.capsule: The unfastened garments, the uncovered head, the covered mouth and the dwelling outside the camp show the sinner disgraced, without defense and banished from the choirs of the saints.
comments.comment: The unfastened garments and the uncovered head would indicate quite clearly that he is disgraced with nothing to hide it. The covering of the mouth means that he has, so to speak, no defense and can say nothing when God charges him with his uncleanness. And the requirement that he leave the camp would again be a type of his no longer living among the choirs of the saints, but, banished as it were from the holy assembly, having no share in any good thing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the signs the leper must bear.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Garments with leprosy picture our state if we are washed by Christ and yet remain in our defilements, so that he hands us over to the fire.
comments.comment: Here again it is perhaps likening our condition to wool and weft, to warp and skins. For who could doubt, or on what grounds, that God takes no account of wool or weft or the rest? We shall grant, then, that among offenses it is most grievous if, after the cleansing and washing that Christ would work in us, we do not get free of our defilements but settle in them to stay. For if Christ washes us and it does us no good, he hands us over to the fire to be punished, just as the priest under the law, when washing had done the weft or the warp no good, then burned it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop and living water of the leper's cleansing paint Christ for us: the living Word, his blood, his incorruptible flesh, the Spirit, baptism and his ascent.
comments.comment: Watch how through these things Christ is painted for us in full: living bird — the living and heavenly Word; slaughtered blood — the Lord’s precious blood in his own body; incorruptible cedar — incorruptible flesh that “did not see corruption” (Acts 2:31); hyssop — the Spirit’s fervor; scarlet — confession of the blood-covenant; living water — baptism’s life-giving grace; sending outside the city — departure from the world and ascent into the heavens; right anointings — that we must become people of contemplation, practice, and journey in the things of God.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of each item in the cleansing rite.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Matthew

comments.capsule: The bodily discharge is an image of the mind that wastes its effort on what it should not and bears no fruit.
comments.comment: … The discharge of the body in a way harms the natural capacity to bear fruit: it lets the supply of seed run out to no purpose, and by slackening the tension in the members it brings about a wasting that is by then, in a sense, involuntary, so that those seized by this condition remain in long and continual defilement. Understand, then, that this is an image, drawn from a visible bodily illness, of what happens to the mind. For the mind too is wasted when it toils most prodigally at what it should not, and spends the effort of its own activity on nothing needful; so it bears no genuine fruit, but is always somehow carried down toward wrongdoing, and, past all restraint, is sick with a descent into baser things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the bodily discharge stands for in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: One who gives up wisdom and justice and spends his natural aptitude for good on baser things suffers a discharge in the spiritual sense.
comments.comment:
But suppose he lets these things [wisdom, self-control, courage and justice] go and becomes no longer wise but foolish and senseless. He does not incline his own will toward those whose habit is to guide people into truth, but prefers to be carried beyond what is fitting and to rush headlong to ruin with those who have made a practice of twisting what is right. He neither holds the best and blameless belief about God, nor travels the road of right conduct without reproach. Would it not, in a way, be accurate to say that such a man suffers a discharge of seed in a spiritual sense, since he spends to no purpose the very things through which he might well have borne fruit for God?

Palladius: I would say so, I assure you.

Cyril: And what if he gives up doing justice and taking pride in the noble deeds of courage, and is seen instead to be unjust and slack, given over to pleasures? Would you not think that he suffers the same sickness as the man with a discharge, since he spends on baser things the natural aptitude for good that he has, and has chosen to lose his spiritual fruitfulness for nothing of any use?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The man with a discharge defiles whatever he touches, to teach us to keep away from the wicked, but only Christ can remove the passions that the law could not.
comments.comment: So the law ordered that one keep as far away as possible from the man with a discharge. By this it teaches us to stay well away from those who have turned toward wickedness, and to shake off with resolve those whom God himself would loathe, as people sick with a continual defilement. For to cling to the wicked is truly not without harm. For it is true, as it is written: ‘Whoever touches pitch will be defiled’ (Sirach 13:1). Indeed, the man with a discharge defiles every article he happens to touch: his bed, skin, vessels, water and wooden utensils (Leviticus 15:4–12). Through these riddles the law hints that a person can share in the uncleanness that is in him even by drawing close to him only in the disposition of the spirit. For it is written: ‘Keep yourself pure, and do not share in the sins of others’ (1 Timothy 5:22). Yet Christ, and the cleansing that comes through him, removes even the passions given up as hopeless, and the sicknesses hidden deep in our thoughts, and simply all the weakness in us; the law could not do this.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The seven days, the washing and the two turtledoves show that cleansing needs good conduct throughout life together with the cleansing of Christ through water and blood.
comments.comment: That the cleansing is drawn out to the seventh day surely signifies that those who have chosen to pass from worldly baseness to the choice of doing what is more fitting must be scoured clean by good conduct throughout their whole life, at every moment they live. For the week, as a measure of time, holds completion and a circling back to the beginning, as when a period has already reached its end. And the law says very well that to our own good conduct there must come, as a necessary addition, the cleansing through Christ and the purification through water. For holy baptism is now understood in the washing of the body and the garments, and with it, clearly, goes the purification through blood. For ‘on the eighth day,’ it says, ‘he shall take for himself two turtledoves or two young pigeons’ (Leviticus 15:14). The eighth day, again, would signify for us the time of the dispensation in the flesh, when Emmanuel, the truly eloquent and most melodious turtledove, endured slaughter for us, and by his own blood has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). That Christ’s death is fragrant in every way (for it was accomplished for the life of the world (John 6:51) and for the abolishing of sin) would be shown by there being two turtledoves, one sacrificed for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering. And that, according to the Scriptures, Christ has become the atoning sacrifice for our sins (1 John 2:2), the law showed by saying: ‘And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord for his discharge’ (Leviticus 15:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the seven days, the washing and the two turtledoves of the cleansing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The words 'unclean until evening' point to Christ's coming at the end of the age, when the filth of sin was at last washed away.
comments.comment: For whoever has offended once, that is, has broken the law at all, even if only in one point and in part, will surely be liable to the charge. So under the law a person is defiled even if he does not go to the extreme of defilement, but is caught having suffered it even in part. Yet he is not cast off entirely; he too is cleansed through water in Christ. Thus the saying that the defiled man is unclean until evening would point very well to the time of Christ’s coming. For Christ came at the end (Hebrews 9:26), when this age had all but reached its very setting; through him and in him we have washed off all the filth that comes from sin, and we who were held fast by our offenses have been set free from charges both small and great. That before the time of his coming it was not possible to wash away defilement (for, according to the Scriptures, no one was justified by the law (Galatians 3:11)), you may learn from its plain saying: ‘He shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 15:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'unclean until the even' points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The law counts a man defiled by any emission, voluntary or involuntary, to show that a person is defiled even when his corruption is only partial and rare.
comments.comment: But it also declares defiled the man who has an emission, whether involuntary or voluntary, springing from the natural impulse. Voluntary, I mean, as in relations with a wife according to the law of marriage; involuntary, again, as perhaps in dreams at night. … For the charges against both are equal, and there is no difference. In the case of the discharge, then, the law described for us an affliction that was, as it were, long and continuous; but in the present case the aim of the law seems to make plain that a person will be defiled even if he does not suffer from complete and total corruption, but is seen to have suffered it only in part and rarely.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The law lifts us from bodily ailments to spiritual thoughts, for once cleansed in Christ we no longer defile the holy tent but worship purely in the churches.
comments.comment: But the law, as though lifting us up to spiritual thoughts and not letting us dwell on the ailments of the flesh (for these were taken up as a type of inward realities grasped by the mind), plainly adds: ‘And you shall make the sons of Israel cautious about their uncleannesses, and they shall not die because of their uncleanness when they defile my tent that is among them’ (Leviticus 15:31). For once we have been cleansed and sanctified through Christ, then, yes then, we draw near truly radiant and shall no longer defile the holy tent; and being pure we shall worship the all-holy God purely as we come to the churches.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law warns the people about their uncleanness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The high priest entered the Holy of Holies only once a year and alone, and no one was permitted to touch him while he was inside.
comments.comment: Now that he entered once a year, Paul made clear, and Moses also makes this same thing plain, speaking this way: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron your brother, and let him not enter at every hour into the inner holy place beyond the veil, before the mercy seat that is on the ark of the testimony, and he will not die" (Leviticus 16:2). And again: "And no person shall be in the tent of testimony when he enters to make atonement in the holy place, until he comes out; and he shall make atonement for himself, and for his house, and for all the assembly of the sons of Israel; and he shall make atonement on the altar that is before the Lord" (Leviticus 16:17). That he did not enter the Holy of Holies continually, and that while he was inside no one was permitted to touch him but had to stand outside by the veil, is clear from these passages.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On Christmas Day

comments.capsule: The one sent away to Azazel is the evil one, whose portion is empty of God.
comments.comment: Again, the one sent away in Leviticus, whom the Hebrew text named Azazel (Leviticus 16:8–10), was no other than he [the evil one]. The one that bore his lot had to be sent away into the wilderness and driven off to avert evil; for all who belong, through their wickedness, to the portion of the worse one stand opposed to those who are of God’s lot, and are deserts, empty of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is meant by the one sent away into the wilderness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VI

comments.capsule: God ordered sacrifices to be offered at the holy tent alone to draw the people from the false worship of Egypt, and whoever sacrificed outside sheds blood, destroying his own soul.
comments.comment: The Lawgiver and Judge, then, ruled that sacrifices must be offered in the holy tent alone by any who chose to offer them. He was drawing them away, I suppose, from the stale false worship, that of Egypt, I mean, where there was much mockery of idols and a most unlovely crowd of falsely named gods, a crowd perhaps unknown even to those who had chosen to worship them; and where sacrifice was left free, to be offered as anyone pleased, just as one of the Greek sages carelessly said: ‘One man sacrificed to one god, another to another.’ Drawing them away, then, from so cold and profane a habit and so senseless a custom, he said again in Leviticus: ‘Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: This is the word which the Lord has commanded, saying: Any man of the sons of Israel, or of those who reside among you, who slaughters a calf or a sheep or a goat in the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness to make it a whole burnt offering or a peace offering to the Lord, acceptable as a fragrant odor; and whoever slaughters outside, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness, and so does not offer a gift to the Lord before the tent of the Lord, it shall be reckoned to that man that he has shed blood; that soul shall be utterly destroyed from its people’ (Leviticus 17:2–4). He says, then, that the one who sacrifices outside the tent sheds blood and will be liable to the charge of murder. For such a man has, as it were, killed himself and destroyed his own soul, since he withdraws it from him who is God by nature, assigns it to stones and wood, and dedicates it to the deceits of demons.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why sacrifice was allowed only at the tent and what 'he hath shed blood' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The law showed that the Church is one and the mystery of Christ is one, so a sacrifice offered outside the holy tent is unlawful.
comments.comment: For the Divine is unapproachable, and a sacrifice without a Levite is unacceptable, since the Levites act as mediators, imitating the Mediator between God and humans, that is, Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). And the law showed plainly that the Church is one and the mystery of Christ is one, and that a sacrifice not performed in the Church is unlawful, or rather is to be rejected and cannot please God; I mean that it showed this by laying down that the sacred rites must not be performed outside the holy tent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Worship belongs to him alone who is God by nature.
comments.comment: So he altogether forbids sacrificing indiscriminately to whomever one wishes, and says, very rightly, that worship must be offered to him alone who is God by nature.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Because the blood is a type of the soul, the law's setting it apart teaches that the soul is immortal, since God willed it to live.
comments.comment:
See, then, how clearly and openly the blood is taken as a type of the soul.

Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: The law, therefore, sets the blood apart and draws it away from the bodies of the slaughtered animals, teaching a true doctrine, one received by us in faith and held in honor in the Churches: I mean that the rational soul of man is immortal, and continues to exist and to think. Death does not destroy it together with earthly bodies; rather, the Creator releases it and sets it free, and exempts it from suffering, having made it a sharer in life. For in the beginning man was made a living soul, when God breathed into him the breath of life; for so it is written (Genesis 2:7). For, I think, we shall be charging the Life that gives life to all things with weakness if we say that what came into life from it perishes together with our temporary bodies. But we shall crown that Life with the most excellent wisdom if we believe that the soul is immortal, since the Creator of all, in whom we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28), has willed that it be so. And this, I suppose, is the reason for the legislation on this point.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Since the soul of a living creature is its blood, and blood turns to flesh and flesh to earth, the soul of animals is something earthy and does not outlast the body.
comments.comment: Since, as it is written, the soul of every living creature is its blood (Leviticus 17:11), and blood when it congeals naturally changes into flesh, and flesh when it decays dissolves into earth, the soul of animals is reasonably something earthy. "Let the earth bring forth a living creature," then. Observe the sequence: soul to blood, blood to flesh, flesh to earth. And again, reversing the steps, go back from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, from blood to soul, and you will find that the soul of animals is earth. Do not think that it is older than the substance of their body, or that it remains after the dissolution of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what 'the soul is the blood' means for animals.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The texts that the soul is the blood have troubled many, but Scripture names things not bodily with the names of bodily things, since a person is two men, outer and inner.
comments.comment: What has pulled them aside is this: The soul of all flesh is blood. And this text has terribly stirred those who have not understood it. And You shall not eat the soul with the flesh; take strong care not to eat blood; you shall not eat the soul with the flesh. This is what has pulled them aside; for the other things that have pulled them aside are far less than the force of the sense in these. … I found that things not bodily are named with the same names as all the bodily things, so that the bodily things belong to the outer man, and the things with the same names as the bodily belong to the inner. Scripture says that the human being is two men: For if our outer man is being destroyed, yet our inner is being renewed day by day; and I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. These two men the apostle everywhere sets out, in each person
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Dialogue with Heraclides

comments.capsule: The righteous alone live in the law's commands, since they have righteousness as their life, while the unjust are like lifeless things moved from outside.
comments.comment: “I will follow your laws,” he says. “For I will have life in them, just as you have said to me: ‘The person who does them will live in them’ (Leviticus 18:5).” Therefore the righteous person alone lives, even if he seems to have died, and the unjust are dead even if they appear to live. For the former have the constitution of life in themselves, namely righteousness, while the latter, not having this, resemble lifeless things moved not by themselves but from outside, because their vital principle is outside, and they have not one life in themselves.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the one who does the commandments will live in them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
comments.work: Fragments on the Psalms

comments.capsule: No one could do the law blamelessly and live by it, so the grace that justifies is better.
comments.comment: “For Moses writes,” he says, “of the righteousness that is from the law, that the person who does it shall live by it” (Romans 10:5; Leviticus 18:5). But there was no one at all who could carry it out blamelessly; for “who will understand transgressions?” (Psalm 19:12). So the grace that justifies is better, and it frees us from the indictment that stands in the law.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'the one who does them shall live' could not save and grace does.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Romans

comments.capsule: Parents must keep their love for their children pure, not selling them for money.
comments.comment: For it is necessary that the ones having begotten also be seen keeping the love unto the children unadulterated, and not bringing them forward unto blood and pollution for the sake of money, nor indeed selling the dignity of nature for gifts.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The 'after the image' of God lies in the inner man, who becomes holy as God is holy and takes up the features of God into his soul.
comments.comment: It remains, then, that the “after the image” of God is to be understood as lying in what we call the inner man, which is being renewed (2 Corinthians 4:16) and is by nature able to become “after the image of the Creator” (Colossians 3:10). This happens when someone becomes “perfect, as the heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), and hears, “You shall be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2), and, learning the words “Be imitators of God” (Ephesians 5:1), takes up into his own virtuous soul the features of God. Then too the body of one who has taken up the things of God into what is “after the image” is a “temple” of God (1 Corinthians 6:19), since he has a soul of this kind and, because of the “after the image”, has God in his soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VI

comments.capsule: Because the deaf and the blind are weak and cannot protect themselves, wrongdoing against them would be hidden but would still show hardness and hate.
comments.comment: And now the law says: ‘You will not speak badly of a deaf person,’ (Leviticus 19:14) wanting somehow, I think, through a riddle to mark that those truly fair in manner must necessarily depart from wrongdoing, even if being able readily to suffer should befall some; for a deaf or blind person is not free of weakness; for they are sick in the things from the body, and have been maimed in the senses—I mean sight and hearing. And the deaf would not hear the one wanting to speak against, nor would a blind person look down upon the one adding a scandal. So then it is nothing hard to escape notice, even if someone should wish to plot against them. But those whom one ought rather to pity, as already weakened from the misfortune from home, will also be caught wronging in addition—crushing with a scandal the blind person who does not know, and with insults the deaf person, sometimes even persuading him to smile as upon good reports, yet striking often even somehow into the most vital things themselves. So the evil-doing upon both would be hidden, if someone should choose, yet it would not pass out from a charge of hardness and of the too-great hate of one another.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
