comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The law commands us not only to refrain from the deed of hatred but to cast out the very disease of the mind, and the justice in Christ goes beyond the law's boundary.
comments.comment: Therefore he has commanded not only to stand off from the deed of the hatred, but also to cast out the very disease of the mind; for the one hating in heart has already been blood-guilty, even if he should not yet stretch out the hand for murder. And Christ also, defining the Gospel justice more severely, was saying: ‘You have heard that it was said for the ancients: You will not murder; yet I say to you that everyone being angered with his brother emptily will be liable to the judgment.’ (Matthew 5:21–22) Therefore the justice in Christ has been stretched beyond the law’s boundary.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law forbids hatred in the heart and not only the deed.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The law says to love the neighbor as yourself, and Christ puts it in the rule of doing to others what you would wish done to you, which is the crown of mutual love.
comments.comment: Therefore the law says, ‘You will love your neighbor as yourself’ (Leviticus 19:18); yet our Lord Jesus Christ introduces for us the law of mutual-loving through as many words as parts, and setting as it were the inborn knowledge and the wish in each as advocate for the law, ‘As many things then as you wish that the humans do for you, these things you also likewise do for them.’ (Matthew 7:12) For if of as many things as someone would pray to obtain, these he should also choose to do for others himself, he will not run off from the aim; yet he will rather walk straight of the love, and will bind on the crown of the mutual-loving.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: Those who lead must stay awake, since the herds and the vineyard of the law stand for the multitude under their hand.
comments.comment: And that it is fitting for those allotted to lead, and leaders of flocks, to stay awake, he again oracled. And what manner of our fairness unto this would become, he hints, saying in Leviticus: ‘You will not make your cattle mount with a differently yoked animal, and you will not sow your vineyard with different seed.’ (Leviticus 19:19) For to herds of goats and sheep, or indeed to a vineyard, one must very well liken the multitude under hand.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: A good shepherd keeps strange animals from his sheep and a good farmer keeps other seed from his vines, and so the rational flock must not be led under the teaching of those not of like faith.
comments.comment: So a virtue of a shepherd is not to let loose upon sheep some animal of another form, so that they fall under somehow foreign mountings, lest it bear something of another nature, and having bent away from the natural good birth present in it; and the caretaker of vineyards, if he should be sensible and have practiced farming most excellently, would never endure the dry of the seeds to grow under the vines themselves, lest, the moisture being spent for them unto the alien, they themselves fall short concerning what is their own. Come then already somehow from an image now unto the spiritual: let us not allow the rational flocks to be led unholily under the sowings of the otherwise-teaching—intelligible ones clearly, and the introductions as in word; for the fruit from dissimilar resolve is very ugly, and the words of those not of like faith would become providers of base conceptions for those who have received them; and we being vineyards, and lying in the order of orchards, it is somehow fitting to be crowned with single-formed fruit, and to decline the double-natured mode. For there is no word unto natural likeness for wheat and clusters. So let there be for none of us a place of alien seeds.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: Cleaning the tree means cutting away the history and the letter to reach the inward fruit of Moses' writing.
comments.comment: For the Writing of Moses seems to us like most well-growing gardens, travailing a many-formed sprout of oracles, and leafy as with trees—the laws upon each. But upon each tree you will clean, he says, its uncleanness—that is, you will cut off the random of the history, and will take around the somehow wooden of the letter, and you will come upon the heart of the plant itself—that is, you will busy-around the inward fruit of what has been oracled, and will make it food.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The three years are the times of Moses, Joshua and the Judges, the fourth that of the prophets, and the fifth that of Christ.
comments.comment: He sets the year unto a time; for first three times have become, according to which the law was still uncleansed-around, weighted down with the thickness of the history, and somehow lying around as random refuse—the shadow. And three times I say there are—that of Moses, that of Joshua, that of the Judges; a fourth time was after those, according to which the bright chorus of the holy prophets grew up. Then the fruit of the law became both holy and praiseworthy. For from holy prophets the things in law began to be set aside, and the things as in shadows not even to be named, and the truth to be preached openly, and the mystery of Christ’s presence to be praised. And at once the forerunner was a neighbor, both crying out and saying: ‘Repent; for the kingdom of the heavens has drawn near.’ (Matthew 3:2) So then in a fourth time toward beginnings of the things in law being thoroughly cleaned it has become, and the fruit was already somehow holy. Yet, in a fifth edible, according to which the presence of Christ is witnessed both through the law and through the prophets.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: What is truly divine does not use irrational animals for knowledge of the future but fills the holiest souls of men and makes them prophets, so the law forbids augury.
comments.comment: What is truly divine does not use irrational animals, nor just any men, for the knowledge of the future, but the holiest and purest souls of men, which it fills with God and makes prophets (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). Therefore, if anything else in the law of Moses is wonderfully said, sayings like these must also be counted among them: “You shall not practise augury, nor watch birds” (Leviticus 19:26); and elsewhere: “For the nations, whom the Lord your God will destroy from before you, will listen to omens and divinations; but to you the Lord your God has not granted it so” (Deuteronomy 18:14); and then, next, he says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law forbids watching birds for omens.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book IV

comments.capsule: The law said to rise before a gray head but set no penalty for failing to do so, and Christ filled up what was lacking.
comments.comment: What was lacking there, he filled up here. The law said, “You shall rise before a gray head,” (Leviticus 19:32) and, “If you see your enemy’s beast fallen under its load, raise it with him.” (Exodus 23:5) If someone transgressed these, the law had defined no punishment. Filling that up, Christ says such a person will be set at nought in the kingdom of God. That is what he calls the least commandment: one on which no penalty was brought for transgression.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Matthew

comments.capsule: Just weights picture the mind that keeps exact equality, but justice is only the law's boundary and the good in Christ goes beyond it.
comments.comment: And with measures and weights and balances he was hurrying very well to equalize the manners of the justice, and very rightly; for a straight and justice-loving mind somehow balances and measures thoroughly the natures of the affairs, and tests the account of the equality, more finely and more exactly than someone would think those testing the coin upon a scale-pan and balance; and he measures out as it were for each of the things contemplated what is most fitting for it, neither loosing the beauty of the exact equality by the excess, nor indeed by the under-bringing toward the less allowing the sufficient as in equality to be counterfeited. Let there then be, he says, just balances and weights, and a just chous; and these would be, I think, as it were some types and clear examples, showing under for us manners through which the account of the exact equality would be searched through for us, and the knowledge of the justice will appear. And understand that the things in law are measured together, and have the justice as a boundary, yet the greater is rich, and the things through Christ run very much beyond. For beyond just is the good—that is, the glory of the citizenship in Christ
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The law forbids following star-prophets and necromancers as unfit for a holy life, and sets death for the medium himself, who has become a snare of death for guiltless souls.
comments.comment: God honors the matter with death, and writes it among the last evils. And he said thus in Leviticus: ‘And a soul which should follow after ventriloquists or enchanters, so as to whore after them, I will set my face upon that soul, and I will destroy it from its people; and you will be holy, because I am holy—Lord your God.’ (Leviticus 20:6) And after other things again: ‘And a man or woman who should become among them a ventriloquist or enchanter, with death let them be put to death, and with stones stone them; they are liable.’ (Leviticus 20:27) For first he refuses that any must love to follow the buffoon star-prophecies, or then necromancies, saying the matter is as far as possible from holy-fitting citizenship, and altogether unfitting for those clinging to God; and he defines death of the second, and says even they themselves are liable; not allowing pity to be allotted from our side to those who have already been driven unto this baseness, as to become a snare of death, and a hunt of guiltless souls, and a door of ruin, and a trapdoor of Hades, and what not of such evils?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: The law against lying with a beast shows as in a type that close dealings with those of another mind bring death both to those who corrupt and to those who willingly accept it.
comments.comment: And in another way also he shows the differently mannered as unjoined and incompatible, and split from communion toward one another, having set beside as a type the most outlandish and altogether strange joining of the rational animal toward what is not such, but of another form and out of tribe. And indeed he also says in Exodus: ‘Whoever should sleep with a beast, you will kill him by death.’ (Exodus 22:19) And more clearly again in Leviticus: ‘And whoever should give his lying in a four-footed animal, let him be put to death by death, and you will kill the four-footed; and a woman who should approach unto every beast to be forced by it, you will kill the woman and the beast; let them be put to death by death; they are liable.’ (Leviticus 20:15-16) For converses and as it were intelligible mixings and joinings toward those for whom it would least be fitting, and for whom the mind has sickened unto unreason the last, are providers of death, both for those who corrupt and for those who endure the corruption as voluntary.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: Under the old law the dead were unclean to the priests, but now, when death is for Christ's sake, the remains of his holy ones are precious and bring a share of sanctification.
comments.comment: When they died in the Jewish manner, the corpses were abominable. When death is for Christ's sake, the remains of his holy ones are precious. Before this, it was said to the priests and the Nazirites: “You shall not be defiled by any dead person,” and, “If anyone touches a corpse, he shall be unclean until evening,” and, “He shall wash his garments” (Leviticus 21:1; Numbers 19:11, 19). But now the one who touches the bones of a martyr receives a certain share of sanctification from the grace that attends the body.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the rule about touching the dead is changed for the martyrs.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Psalm 115

comments.capsule: Nothing in Christ is profane, so the high priest keeps from the dead altogether, while the other priests were allowed to mourn their nearest kin as human beings who stumble.
comments.comment: That there is nothing profane in Christ in any way is hinted at indirectly when the law says that the high priest must keep away from what is dead, going near no dead person at all, even though this means setting aside the honor owed to father, mother and brothers. See how wise the law is, and how seriously it takes the good order that befits what it signifies. In the case of the other priests it made allowance for nature, and for the dead who were very close and of their own blood it allowed the consecrated to carry out the customary rites without blame (Leviticus 21:1–3). It was not greatly concerned there about a fault against the shadow. For in that case the charges were written with us in view, and the type pointed to human beings; and if some defilement should attach to them, there is nothing strange in that. ‘For we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2), and in us our nature has fallen sick with wrongdoing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The law lets priests share the grief of their nearest kin out of reverence for nature, but not to excess, for they are priests of life and offer the sacrifice that undoes death.
comments.comment: Yet the law allows the consecrated to incur defilement without blame for father and mother, for children and brothers, and indeed for close kin, by going even to their lifeless bodies, out of reverence for nature; and in this it overlooks wrongs that are wrongs only as types, so that those who are known to God might not seem hard, haughty and unfeeling; and indeed the law says plainly: ‘Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you’ (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). In another way too, and for another reason, we say the consecrated are barred from mourning. For they are priests of life, and offer the sacred gifts to God for the undoing of death (for the death of Christ, foreshadowed through sheep and calves, is the undoing of death); how then would it be fitting for them to be weighed down with grief over death? So too the inspired Paul writes plainly to those baptized into Christ in the hope of life and resurrection: ‘I say this so that you may not grieve as the rest do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus, and will raise them with us’ (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The law, then, allowed the consecrated to go to those of their very closest kin who had died. But it sets a measure on the matter, and does not let them undo what most befits them by going to excess, beyond what is needed, so that the revered dignity of the priesthood may not be wronged. For it keeps them from baring their heads as others do, and from shaving off the beard to the disgrace of the face; and it commands them not even to entertain the thought of the impious acts of pagan frenzy, I mean the gashes cut into the flesh (Leviticus 21:5). For there is nothing unreasonable in sharing the grief of one’s own family; but to lose all decorum would be unseemly and quite senseless. ‘For let all things,’ he says, ‘be done decently and in order’ (1 Corinthians 14:40). And the Savior himself has commanded us as well that the things of God must be honored above even duties to parents, as the old law required of the priests; for he says: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Priests must avoid not only plain evils but anything that brings a name for wickedness, and the harlot daughter burned with fire is read as the Synagogue that left the spiritual Bridegroom.
comments.comment:
Yet the woman cast out by her husband is by no means free of blame either, for she would not be driven from her husband’s home without some cause. Those who have been brought into so holy a ministry, then, must keep away not only from evils whose guilt is plain and open to view, but also, I think, from anything that might bring with it a name for wickedness, a poor opinion of them, or the indecency of lying under a great many suspicions.

The passage also seems to hint at the misfortune of the Synagogue of the Jews. Because she played the harlot with many shepherds, as it is written (Jeremiah 3:1), Christ did not receive her into spiritual fellowship: Christ the wholly pure priest, who offers himself to the Father for us as a choice gift, who is holy with us in his humanity, although he himself sanctifies the whole creation, since he is God from God. He made the mystery plainer still when he said: ‘And if the daughter of a priest profanes herself by playing the harlot, she profanes the name of her father; she shall be burned with fire.’ (Leviticus 21:9) For the Synagogue of the Jews has been given over to the flame as unholy and profane, because she followed the opinions of the scribes and Pharisees and devoted her whole mind to the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9). So it was very just that she heard the prophet say: ‘How have you become a harlot, faithful city of Zion, full of justice?’ (Isaiah 1:21) Having played the harlot, then, and utterly disregarded the spiritual Bridegroom from above, she has become fuel for the fire.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The high priest's turban and untorn garments hint that Christ's priesthood and kingship can never be lost and that Life has nothing to do with grief over death.
comments.comment: You see plainly how Emmanuel, the Christ, is named here, still in types, in the person of Aaron. For he who is himself the priest perfect in every way was anointed with the Spirit, according to the Scriptures (Acts 10:38). So the glory of his priesthood is one he can never lose. For ‘he shall not take the turban,’ it says, ‘from his head’ (Leviticus 21:10); that is, he will not lay aside the dress that befits a priest. For it was said to the Savior and Redeemer of all: ‘You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.’ (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:17) ‘The former priests were many in number, because death prevented them from continuing; but he, because he remains for ever, holds his priesthood permanently. Therefore he is also able to save completely those who draw near to God through him.’ (Hebrews 7:23–25) This is what the inspired Paul wrote. So the fact that the turban is never taken from his head would hint that his priesthood can never be lost. And if the reading were ‘He shall not take the mitre from his head,’ you will readily understand that his kingship is perpetual and cannot be shaken; for the mitre, with the golden band across the front of the brow, would be a symbol of rule and kingship. ‘Nor shall he tear his garments,’ it says (Leviticus 21:10). Some people are in the habit of doing this over the dead, but such a thing is wholly foreign to Christ. For the Life would be the last to suffer grief at a death. The Life has nothing at all to do with what is dead; rather, it is itself the undoing of death and the overthrow of corruption. So the Savior once rebuked those who wanted to wail over the little daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, saying: ‘Go away, and do not weep, for the girl is not dead but asleep.’ (Matthew 9:24; Luke 8:52) For it was truly out of place for them to shed tears as over a dead girl when the Life of all, that is, Christ, was present. And if he wept over Lazarus (John 11:35), we say that this was the fruit of his tender love, and the compassion that divine gentleness has toward us. For our nature, under the tyranny of death, was being pitied, and his tear was its release from that suffering.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the high priest's turban and untorn garments mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Christ is free of all profanation, so the priest's virgin bride is the Church, and Christ joins himself only to chaste and pure souls.
comments.comment: For Christ is free of all profanation; he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21) and is beyond all defilement, or rather, he is all radiance and spiritual purity. He remains within all holiness, even if, here at least, its brightness has grown faint, because he stands firm on the laws of his own nature and is always the same and unchanging. This, I think, is what is meant by ‘He shall not go out of the holy place, and shall not profane what is consecrated to his God.’ (Leviticus 21:12) He says very rightly that he must take a virgin as his wife into the fellowship of marriage (Leviticus 21:13–14), and he declares the woman who has been driven out unfit for him. She may also stand as a type of the Synagogue of the Jews, for she has been cast out of union with him, and he says of her through the prophet’s voice: ‘She is not my wife, and I am not her husband.’ (Hosea 2:2) But Paul betrothed the Church from the Gentiles to Christ as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2), without spot or wrinkle, or rather holy and blameless (Ephesians 5:27). Taken in this way, of the Church from the Gentiles and of the mother of the Jews, the riddle would be true and the type not without beauty. But if someone wishes to apply the force of these ideas fittingly to each individual, we say that Christ has no union with profane and unholy souls; but with souls that are wholly chaste and pure, like virgins, he is joined spiritually, makes them fruitful, and calls them his own kin. For ‘whoever does the will of my Father in heaven,’ he says, ‘is my brother and my sister and my mother.’ (Matthew 12:50)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the high priest's virgin bride signifies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: God holds in honor the blameless, and this law reaches the whole sacred family, now those sanctified in Christ, the true High Priest.
comments.comment: … what he holds in honor is the blameless: what suffers no corruption from any quarter, what is sound, so to speak, in virtue and strong in sanctification, what has trained itself thoroughly to win approval through patient endurance, and is always quick to understand. That is why he makes his law on this point extend to the whole family, showing the sacred and chosen race to be his own and free of all alloy: then, in the tribe of Levi and the blood of Aaron; but now in those who have been sanctified in Christ, the great and true High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), to whom we have been joined through the Spirit, and so have been shown to be sharers and partakers of his own nature (2 Peter 1:4).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The Creator does not blame bodily infirmity that comes against the will, so the bodily blemishes of the priest stand for the many forms of the passions of the soul, which are hateful to God.
comments.comment: Blame and indictment may sometimes fall on those whose minds turn aside to evil of their own free choice, and who have come to prize a leaning toward outrage of any kind. But to censure infirmities of the flesh, which come about by nature and against the will, is, I think, harsh and unfeeling, and not free from the charge of crassness. From this, then, we can understand that the Creator of all would not have indicted human nature for causes beyond the will, nor would he have sent away from the ministry appointed to him, as unholy, a man who is sick in body. Rather, once more, by a type drawn from bodily things he refines our minds toward his subtler purposes: he hints at the many forms of the passions in the soul and gives us to understand that such a thing is hateful to God. Did not the inspired Paul also say that those chosen for the priesthood must be attended by an honorable verdict on every quality that wins admiration? ‘So that the man of God may be complete,’ he says, ‘fully equipped for every good work’ (2 Timothy 3:17). He insisted, too, and very clearly, that the bishop must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and he was very exacting in these matters. … The word is firm, the decree severe. For the law was laid down not only for those born of Aaron at that time; it reaches to the whole family and to every priestly line, and it extends through all time. That, I think, is what ‘of your family throughout your generations’ makes clear. For what is not blameless is always unacceptable to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why bodily blemishes bar a man from the priesthood.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The blind man is the man wholly without understanding and the lame man the one whose eagerness for good deeds is broken and feeble, and both are unfit for sacred service.
comments.comment: Let us rather speak of what we need for knowledge and spiritual contemplation, getting beneath the coarse surface of the history. By ‘blind,’ then, he seems to mean the man who is very foolish and utterly senseless. For what the eye is to the earthly body, the mind may be called in the soul. It is lit up by the divine light, it opens its eyes to that pure beauty itself, and with the fine and nimble movements, as it were, of its thoughts it springs up readily toward exact belief, and knows how to keep from missing right doctrine. This, I think, is what is said in the Proverbs: ‘Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids nod toward what is just’ (Proverbs 4:25). And somewhere it is also said to the mother of the Jews, who did not see rightly: ‘See, your eyes are not good, nor is your heart; they are set on nothing but your greed, on innocent blood, to shed it, on your wrongdoings, and on murder, to commit them’ (Jeremiah 22:17). So the one who is blind in the spiritual sense is unfit for sacred service, that is, the man wholly without understanding, maimed in mind and judgment. Unfit as well is the lame man, that is, one who does not know how to walk uprightly and has no strength to walk soundly. For blindness, as I said just now, is a sign of utter lack of understanding; lameness, in turn, is a sign of a movement and eagerness that is, as it were, broken and feeble, such as a man may show toward each of the things he has to do.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The stunted nose is a mind that cannot discern between better and worse, and the clipped ear is hearing that turns away from the truth.
comments.comment: Besides these, the law said that the man with a stunted nose must be rejected, and with him the man with a clipped ear. One might apply to them an explanation like this. By the sense of smell we test what smells foul and what is most fragrant, among things, I mean, whose nature has received the power to give off a smell; and that sense is very discerning, both of what can give delight and of what perhaps is not of that sort but otherwise, ranking, as it were, among the worse. The human mind, I would say, if it is sound in what belongs to it, sets out vigorously to discern the quality of things and will make an exact test of each; and like an excellent money-changer, testing everything, holding fast to what is good and keeping away from every form of evil, as it is written (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22), it will win high approval. For it rejects as counterfeit whatever among our deeds is in any way shameful and falsely stamped, and it would readily accept what is profitable and better. The flattened nose, then, signifies what is not altogether healthy and sound in perception, the faculty by which we discern each thing excellently, give the better verdict to the best and the worse to the more shameful, and are, and are called, wise and quick-witted and everything else of that kind. For the smell, rising as it were to the mind, is the real quality, so to speak, of the things the mind perceives. And to have the ear clipped would suggest, as it seems to me, being hard of hearing. For when the hearing is clipped, I would grant that the affliction is an obedience given only in part, not wholly answering to the rein, or else the inability to listen blamelessly to sacred things, and above all to the sacred writings. Some indeed do just that, most thoughtlessly turning the soul’s readiness to hear toward things it should not. These would be, in the words of the most wise Paul, those who have itching ears and turn their hearing away from the truth (2 Timothy 4:3–4), who devote themselves to spirits of error (1 Timothy 4:1), and who have turned aside to profane, empty talk (1 Timothy 6:20). So the man with a clipped ear would suggest the maiming of the inward and spiritual hearing, and its corruption from rightness into something worse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The man with a broken foot or hand does not carry his deeds through soundly, and to do good not rightly is put on the same footing as to do no good at all.
comments.comment: [By the man with a broken foot or hand the law means] … the one who cannot carry his deeds through to the full, and whose walk, that is, his activity, is not entirely beyond reproach: I mean in conduct and in a life lived fully by the law. These again would be those who do the work of the Lord carelessly, against whom the voice of the prophet has pronounced woe (Jeremiah 48:10), or those who pursue what is just, but not justly, as it is written (Deuteronomy 16:20). Notice that even a moderate injury to the leg is put on the same level as spiritual and complete lameness, and is counted as the same thing. For not doing good rightly will be placed on the same footing as being unable to do any good at all. One may fairly see in lameness the ‘not at all,’ and in the crushed limb the ‘not soundly.’
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The hunchback is bent toward earthly things and the blotched man is the one who sins openly and does not hide his faults.
comments.comment: Again, he lists the hunchback, the man with blotches, and the man with bleary eyes among the most unfit (Leviticus 21:20). We say the hunchback is the one who is, as it were, bent over: he looks downward in mind, leans toward the passions of the flesh, and fixes his eye on earthly things (clearly, the eye of the mind), and has at last come to such a frame of mind that he hates to be set upright, I mean, for the duty of setting the mind on things above (Colossians 3:2). Under this would fall the charges against the Jews, of whom it is written: ‘Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back for ever’ (Psalm 69:23; Romans 11:10). The man with blotches is one who has what is called a blotch on his very forehead. This is a kind of sickness that darkens the surface of the skin. It takes from those who suffer it even the chance of staying hidden, since it breaks out on the very brows and spreads over the whole face. Such a man, then, is blotched in body; but in a spiritual sense he points to the man who is unseemly openly and without concealment, who has, as it were, no clean face, but whose ugliness of life is plain to all, so that perhaps he does not even know what one of the wise rightly said: ‘The wise will hide their own shames.’ … The law, then, calls such a man blotched, since he neither knows how to hide nor will bear to hide the sickness and passion that has come upon him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The man with bleary eyes has understanding but cannot see soundly, since seeing is of no use unless one chooses to see rightly.
comments.comment: [The man with bleary] … eyes is the one who is by no means deprived of sight, yet cannot see soundly. Such would be those who have understanding, but in whom no choice to think rightly is seen. For some, he means, see what is good, yet turn the bent of their own wills aside toward what they ought not; others, though they could have a share in right doctrine, all but ruin their own minds themselves: they throw themselves into a most unlovely hunt after notions and accept nothing sound in their belief about God. Such above all are the children of the heretics, and the Jews besides, who believe that the Father is God, yet most foolishly thrust away the One who has come forth from him, the Son by nature. So the word proclaimed by the voice of the prophet is true of them: ‘They have eyes, and they do not see’ (Jeremiah 5:21). For seeing is of no use unless care is taken that one sees soundly, just as we rightly said that lameness and the crushed foot are placed on the same footing. For it will make no difference at all whether one cannot walk at all or perhaps does not walk soundly, meaning, of course, the path of conduct and the road of deeds.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The man with one testicle is the half-man, effeminate or not wholly strong, while one devoted to God should bring him courage and strength no one can mock.
comments.comment: Next, as I at least think, he means by the man with only one testicle the half-man, the one who has, as it were, been cut off from full manliness. ‘For neither the sexually immoral,’ he says, ‘nor the soft will inherit the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 6:9–10). By this he names the effeminate, because, though they were given the nature of a man, they belie their manhood: they grow soft in mind and body and willingly break themselves down into feebleness and womanish ways. It is likely, again, that the man with one testicle points to something else as well. For it is usual to call a ‘man’ one who is strong and well knit, and fully able to accomplish whatever he may choose. So a half-man may fittingly be understood as one who is not wholly strong, nor fully vigorous for what befits him. For it is not fitting that one devoted to God should bring him a courage cut short and a strength maimed, so as to be weak in part; rather he should ‘act like a man and be strong,’ as it is written (1 Corinthians 16:13), with an eagerness that no one can fault or mock.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The raging itch and the spreading rash are passions that exceed all measure or keep creeping outward, and the law wants us to check them before they lead to ruin.
comments.comment:
We should liken the raging itch to the most monstrous of the passions, which pour down on the mind in sharper, more acrid streams and pass all measure, and which begin in pleasure but end in bitterness. Or would you not say that in each kind of sin the evil is seen in a measured form and also beyond measure?

Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: The man overcome by bodily pleasure: could he not suffer this both moderately and beyond measure? Some are only overcome, and are sick in a restrained way; others reach the height of the evil and are sick with a pleasure that rages out of control, so that they slip even beyond the passions that belong to nature.

Palladius: I understand what you mean.

Cyril: So in each of the evils, whatever has strayed monstrously beyond reason, and beyond the measures that are usual and common among most people, may be called the raging itch. The spreading rash, besides, is any passion at all that keeps creeping outward over a wider area and never stops growing worse. But the divine law wants us to check the passions that befall us and to reduce them. You will understand something of this kind when you hear: ‘If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put an end to great sins’ (Ecclesiastes 10:4). For passions left unrebuked always creep toward a more shameful state; they seize heart and mind and lead to utter ruin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The man with a blemish may share the holy food as one who is sick, for the putting away of evil and recovery of health, but is barred from the altar.
comments.comment: So the man listed under ‘blemish’ is admittedly unfit for sacred service. Yet he is not barred from sharing in the holy food. ‘For he shall eat of the holy things,’ he says, ‘but he shall not go in to the veil, and he shall not come near the altar’ (Leviticus 21:22–23). For those who are still subject to weaknesses hidden within the mind may share in the blessing of Christ, not as ranked among the saints, for growth in holiness, for steadiness of mind, and for a steadfastness firmly grounded in all that is best, but in the way that suits the sick: for the putting away of evil, the ending of sin, the putting to death of pleasures, and the recovery of spiritual health. For since Christ is a new creation, according to the Scriptures (2 Corinthians 5:17), we too therefore receive him into ourselves through his holy flesh and blood, so that, refashioned through him and in him for newness of life (Romans 6:4), we may put off the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit, as it is written (Ephesians 4:22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the blemished priest may eat the holy food but not approach the altar.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The leper and the man with a discharge stand for those held by works of deadness, who must withdraw from the holy things until cleansed, as Paul says each must examine himself.
comments.comment: So the leper and the man with a discharge, that is, the one held fast by the works of deadness (and the works of deadness would be the passions of the flesh), and the one who does not keep his inner fruitfulness uncorrupted, the hidden fruitfulness of the mind, must withdraw, he says, from the holy things until he is cleansed (Leviticus 22:4). For as the inspired Paul said, ‘Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning his body’ (1 Corinthians 11:27, 29). ‘But let a man,’ he says, ‘examine himself, and then let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup’ (1 Corinthians 11:28).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Bodily touch does not defile the soul, but the law teaches in figures that whoever clings to those sick with passions shares their defilement through a shared will or deeds.
comments.comment: … a touch of the body will not defile a person’s soul. But the law is spiritual (Romans 7:14), and once again it teaches us in figures that those who are guilty of the passions of the soul are unclean, charged with defilement; and those who touch them, or cling to them, are defiled together with them, clearly by the bond of a shared will or shared deeds. For ‘bad company ruins good character’ (1 Corinthians 15:33), and ‘a believer has no share with an unbeliever’ (2 Corinthians 6:15), and light is hostile to darkness and can make no terms with it (2 Corinthians 6:14). … He showed at once that to be sick with the most outrageous of the passions will be grievous not for the sick alone, but that those who come to share their mind and judgment will be defiled with stains no less than theirs, for he added: ‘Whoever touches any unclean creeping thing, it will defile him, or a man through whom he will be defiled by any of his uncleanness; the soul that touches them shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 22:5–6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the law on touching the unclean teaches.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The unclean man waits until evening because nothing before Christ was cleansed, and those washed in baptism, as the sun sets, have the living bread from heaven.
comments.comment:
See, then, Palladius, that the putting away of all filth and the release from the charges against us could come about in us in no other way than through Christ alone, and at the time of his coming.

Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: He showed that everything before the coming of the Only-begotten was unpurified and still stained, and had no share in life, when he said, ‘He shall be unclean until evening, and he shall not eat of the holy things’ (Leviticus 22:6). Or did not Emmanuel come in the last times of the age?

Palladius: Yes, that is plain.

Cyril: And we have been given life by eating the bread that is truly holy and from heaven (John 6:32–33), that is, Christ, when the time had come to its end, as though the sun were setting and bringing the measure of time to a close in evening. … This is why the one who is defiled remains unclean until evening and has no share in the holy and life-giving food, while he waits for the time of cleansing. But once he has washed in water and the sun has set, he is clean, and he has the bread from heaven as his own. For to those who have been sanctified through water, I mean in holy baptism, it has been granted, as it were, to be blessed through Christ; and he himself is the living bread, and he again is the one who came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:51; John 6:33).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The foreigner, the sojourner and the hired servant are shut out from the holy food as those who do not yet believe, who live for the world, or who make godliness a means of gain.
comments.comment:
He has defined who would be worthy of the blessing and able to press on toward it, and he makes clear who ought to be driven away from the sacred food, saying: ‘And no foreigner shall eat holy things; a sojourner with a priest or a hired servant shall not eat holy things. But if a priest acquires a person bought with silver, he shall eat of his bread, and those born in his house, they too shall eat of his bread’ (Leviticus 22:10–11).

He shuts out the foreigner, the man of another race, as defiled and still unwashed, that is, the one who has not yet believed and does not know the true God. For how could those who cannot be bound through a spiritual and inward kinship to Christ, the great and true Priest, share in his bread? For we will not give what is holy to the dogs, and no one would throw the spiritual pearls before swine, according to the Savior’s own words (Matthew 7:6). So the foreigner has no share at all. With him he joins the sojourner and the hired servant. These again, in my own view, would be those who live for the world and conduct their lives by it, and have made the earth their homeland, as it were, by minding only the things of the flesh; but in their love for Christ they are only sojourners, living, as it were, in bare faith alone. As far as words go, they are good and reasonable, but in the deeds and ways of true piety they have strayed very far indeed. The hired servants, in turn, would perhaps be those who chose even the bare act of believing not out of reverence for the truth, but hunting for the favor of certain people as a kind of wage for seeming to be Christians; who fawn to win the attentions of those able to benefit them; who make godliness a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:5) and a cover for love of profit, and put on fair words like a mask.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the foreigner, sojourner and hired servant stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Those acquired by silver or born in the house are the genuine believers, members of the household in spirit and bought with a price.
comments.comment: But he said that the sharing of the holy things must be left open to the members of the household. For those born in the priests’ households will eat, he says, and anyone they may happen to buy. By ‘acquired’, ‘bought with silver’ and ‘born in the house’ he means, I take it, the one who is genuine in faith, a member of the household in spirit, and bought with a price, as the blessed Paul says (1 Corinthians 6:20). For, as it is written, ‘Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us’ (Galatians 3:13).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: A priest's daughter married to a foreigner loses her share, which pictures the soul that has been born again but joins herself to people who are not holy.
comments.comment:
He further commands that if the daughter of a priest is married to a foreign man, she shall not eat of the firstfruits of the holy things (Leviticus 22:12). He has plainly honored the member of the household by allowing him to share in the holy things as one who is genuine. … For just as in the passages already read he made the leper unclean, and with him the man with a discharge, and made the one who came near them, joined to them, as it were, by touch, a sharer in their defilement and uncleanness, so here too he says that the priest’s daughter, even if she happens to have a holy kinship, will gain nothing from it when she is joined to another, that is, to a foreigner, one who is in no way akin to her and not of the blood of Israel. Let this, then, be the historical sense.

But when we carry the law over into spiritual contemplation, we say that by the priest’s daughter he means the soul that has been born again of water and the Spirit (John 3:5) by the power of Christ, and called through faith to sanctification. Yet even such a soul, he says, may have no share in the holy things if she is married to a foreign man, that is, if she joins herself to people who are not truly holy and have no spiritual bond with God. For bodies the manner of union would be bodily, but for spirits it is spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rule on the priest's daughter married to a stranger.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The priest's daughter married to a man of another race is the Synagogue of the Jews, who held God's commandments as nothing and kept the teachings of men.
comments.comment: And I think the lawgiver also hints at something else to us through these laws. For he foretells, as it were, the falling away of the Synagogue of the Jews, the punishment that follows it, and the kindness that will be shown to her in due time, which by the mercy of God brings her back and restores her to what she was at the beginning. For ‘a priest’s daughter,’ he says, ‘if she is married to a man of another race, shall not eat of the firstfruits of the holy things’ (Leviticus 22:12). For as far as teaching and instruction go, the inspired Moses became a kind of father to the Synagogue of the Jews. She was, then, a priest’s daughter; for Moses too was a minister of sacred rites, since he was of the blood and tribe of Levi. But this man’s daughter became the wife of a man of another race. For she held what God had laid down to be worth almost nothing, and, in a manner of speaking, disregarded the seeds from above; she has studied teachings that are the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9; Isaiah 29:13), and she bears fruit for the opinions of others. That is why God reproached her, saying to her through the voice of Jeremiah: ‘Lift up your eyes and look straight ahead, and see: where have you not defiled yourself? By the roadsides you sat waiting for them like a lonely crow, and you defiled the land with your prostitution and your wickedness; and you had many shepherds, to your own stumbling’ (Jeremiah 3:2–3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The widowed priest's daughter who returns to her father's house pictures the soul that has strayed and then repents, and whom the Father gathers again with the bread from heaven.
comments.comment: Right after this he laid down another law, close to the first; it runs as follows: ‘And if a priest’s daughter becomes a widow, cast out, and has no offspring, she shall return to her father’s house as in her youth; she shall eat of her father’s bread’ (Leviticus 22:13). The historical sense, I think, is plain; but we must go on to the inner and hidden meanings. For if, he says, a soul should be cast off as condemned, and is seen from then on to be without a husband, that is, without the spiritual Bridegroom, and bears no fruit of virtue, let her hurry her steps back to what she was at the beginning, and let her return quickly to her own father’s house, seeking, that is, through repentance, to belong to God; and then she will eat of his bread. Nothing prevents us from applying the force of these words also to those we spoke of a moment ago. For if, he says, a sacred and holy soul, carried away by profane men, should slip into error and take in the defilement of alien doctrines, and so become like a widow, sent away from God, but should then somehow come to her senses and learn what she has slipped into, let her return to the Father. For he receives those who have strayed, if they prove clean of the unholy seeds sown in them, and if they carry no trace of the foulness of those who led them astray; and so he gathers them into one flock with the holy worshipers, setting himself before them as bread from heaven, their life-giving food (John 6:32–33).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the widowed daughter's return as a picture of repentance.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The Synagogue, widowed and cast out for rejecting Christ, will return to her father's house and share in the blessing, as the prophet says.
comments.comment: For she utterly refuses the Bridegroom who comes from above, from God the Father, and gives heed to the words of the scribes and Pharisees. So she has become the wife of a man of another race, and for that reason she has remained without a share in the holy things; for she did not eat the bread from heaven, that is, Christ (John 6:32). You see the charges, and the punishment that Christ at once brought on those guilty of such impiety. Now observe also how they have been shown mercy and been brought back to what they were at the beginning. ‘A priest’s daughter,’ he says, ‘if she becomes a widow, cast out, and there is no offspring in her, shall return to her father’s house as in her youth, and shall eat of her father’s bread’ (Leviticus 22:13). For the Synagogue of the Jews was shown to be a widow and cast out because of her impiety toward Christ; she has remained in sins, possessing none of the spiritual goods, and has continued so for a long time. But she will return to her father’s house; for she too will be called to God through faith; with us she will claim as Father the Creator of all things, and so would come to share in the blessing of Christ. The prophet’s words will make this mystery clear to you as well; for he spoke thus: ‘For the sons of Israel will remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or oracles; and afterward the sons of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and their king, and they will be filled with awe at the Lord and at his good things in the last days’ (Hosea 3:4–5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: A priest who kept a whole offering for himself was charged with eating holy things, and one who did so in ignorance repaid it with a fifth added, so those in charge of sacred things must claim nothing before the sacrifice.
comments.comment: … So it was necessary that the portion of what was brought be consecrated to God, according to the law that fitted each offering, and that the ministers be sustained with the rest of the body of the sacrifice. But if anyone kept back the whole gift entirely for himself and spent it on his own needs, having burned none of it, he was charged under the law as one who had eaten holy things. This is just what the sons of Eli the priest did: they seized and profaned the sacred offerings before the sacrifices were made, and said most impiously to those who came to sacrifice, ‘Give meat for the priest to roast’ (1 Samuel 2:15). But those deeds, being deliberate and plainly insolent, were punished accordingly. ‘But if,’ he says, ‘someone, either overtaken by forgetfulness or not knowing exactly what the laws require, should do any such thing, let him bear a penalty: let him repay the same amount without fail, and let him add to it a fifth as well,’ that is, the fifth part of the value; ‘for in this way he will be cleared of the charges and will ward off the harm that comes from ignorance’ (Leviticus 22:14; Leviticus 5:15–16). If, then, what is done in ignorance is not free from indictment, what would anyone think of what is done out of madness and audacity? Those, then, who have the care of the sacred things must refrain from seeking to claim anything for themselves before the sacrifice; otherwise let them know that, having committed grave offenses, they will incur punishment and come under the wrath of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what eating the holy thing unwittingly means and why a fifth is added.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Even the consecrated may not treat the holy things as common, for only part of each offering went up on the altar and the rest fed the priests.
comments.comment:
He made it plain at once that even for those who are truly consecrated it is not without penalty to treat the holy things as if they were for common use, and to think they differ in no way from other things; for he says: ‘And a man who eats the holy things in ignorance shall add a fifth more to it and give the holy thing to the priest; and he shall not profane the holy things of the sons of Israel which they set apart for the Lord, and they will bring on themselves the iniquity of trespass when they eat their holy things; for I am the Lord who sanctifies them’ (Leviticus 22:14–16).

Palladius: I do not quite understand what you mean.

Cyril: You will learn it very clearly; there is nothing hard about it. The offerings dedicated for a pleasing aroma, a calf, say, or a sheep, were carried up to the altar in part, once the entrails, the feet and head, the fat, and sometimes the kidneys too had been taken out; and with what remained they fed the priests.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The animal with a cut tongue is the one who cannot speak the word of faith, and those with warts or mange are souls whose passions spread and grow worse.
comments.comment:
The animal with a cut tongue, as I think, is the one who does not know how to speak rightly and has no strength to proclaim, as it is written, ‘the word of faith which we preach’ (Romans 10:8), ‘the appeal to God from a good conscience’ (1 Peter 3:21). Yet the prophet will make plain that at the coming of Christ they will throw off this kind of disease too, when he says: ‘And the stammering tongues will quickly learn to speak peace’ (Isaiah 32:4). So the one with a cut tongue is the one who still stammers and has not yet been taught to speak the peace that comes to us from above and from the Father, that is, Christ (Ephesians 2:14), or the things concerning him.

The animals with warts, with festering mange, or with scabs (Leviticus 22:22) we take to be those who have within themselves a mind in the grip of passion and are deeply sick with the corruption that lies in sin, yet never consider that they ought to reduce them, but rather let them creep on toward what is more shameful and spread toward what is worse. For warts and festering mange and scabs plainly always grow, tend somehow toward a worse state, and little by little spread over the whole body. So too are the passions in our souls that are not cut short but always race on toward the worse, as if with a rush that nothing holds back.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The animal with ears cut off is the person hard to persuade who will not listen, and the one with no tail is unseemly and lacks beauty.
comments.comment:
The animal with its ears cut off, and besides it the one with a docked tail (Leviticus 22:23), would signify the person who is hard to persuade and will not listen, and the one who is not seemly in every respect. Or is the harm not to the hearing, for those whose ear has been cut off?

Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: And animals that have no tail, would you yourself grant that they have the finest form? Not at all; for in themselves they are badly marred by unsightliness. So the person hinted at indirectly, as it were by an animal that has no tail, is unseemly and lacks beauty.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The bruised and cut male are those with a name for manly courage who do not actively pursue virtue and bear no fruit.
comments.comment: The law also rejects what is male by nature but cannot do what males do; I mean the bruised and the cut (Leviticus 22:24). Such again would be those who have a reputation for the manly courage that leads to virtue, yet are not actually active in pursuit of the glories of virtue; they are dry, as it were, and barren, and in many ways robbed of the power to bear fruit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Gifts may not be offered through a foreigner's hand, which signifies that the Father can be approached through Christ alone, our High Priest and Mediator.
comments.comment: Besides these things the law further declared that it is abominable to offer sacrifices to God through a foreign hand as well, saying: ‘And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer the gifts to the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 22:25). By this it is signified in type that the Father can be approached through Christ alone. For he is our truly unblemished and great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), the Mediator in the divine economy (1 Timothy 2:5). For as the inspired Paul writes: ‘In him we have gained access in the Spirit to the Father’ (Ephesians 2:18). So those who choose to consecrate their own souls to God the Father, with Christ as Mediator, ought to be free of blemish. ‘For you shall be holy,’ he says, ‘as I am holy’ (Leviticus 11:44).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no offering is taken from a foreigner's hand.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The newborn animal is kept seven days under its mother because what is immature is not yet acceptable, and from the eighth day, the day of the resurrection, everything in Christ is a gift pleasing to God.
comments.comment:
So he does not allow a lamb that is newborn and still at the breast to be slaughtered, showing that what is still immature and, so to speak, small and weak in understanding is not yet holy, and for this reason is still unacceptable to God. … For the animals that are brought and dedicated to God must, he says, be seven days under their mother, but from the eighth day on they will be a gift, and an offering by fire to God.

Palladius: Your point is not very clear.

Cyril: Do you not say that the eighth day is the day of the Savior’s resurrection, and the beginning, as it were, of a new age, once the time of the law, figured in the first seven days, has passed by?

Palladius: I do.

Cyril: Then whatever belongs, so to speak, to the time of the law, that is, whatever lies in worship according to the flesh, is still unholy and cannot yet be offered; but from now on everything in Christ, on the eighth day and after, is already a gift and well pleasing to God. For the calling in Christ has no end, and its beginning is the resurrection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why an animal must stay seven days under its mother and be accepted on the eighth day.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Every solemn assembly is a feast, but not every feast is an assembly.
comments.comment: “These are the feasts of the Lord” (Leviticus 23:2). Every cheerful day on which it has been prescribed to do certain special things as on a holy day, beyond what is done on the remaining days, is called a feast. But not every feast is a solemn assembly; rather, according to the name, it is when people are gathered together from everywhere to the same place. So a solemn assembly is also a feast, but a feast is not necessarily also a solemn assembly. For example, Sabbaths and New Moons are feasts, but Unleavened Bread, the days of the Weeks, and Tabernacles are not only feasts but also solemn assemblies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between a feast and a solemn assembly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Leviticus

comments.capsule: The first sheaf sketches the resurrection, when human nature flourished again in Christ.
comments.comment: The season of new things sketches the mystery of the resurrection; for human nature flourished again in Christ first, wiping off corruption and casting away at last the aging that comes from sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the offering of the firstfruits signifies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: The time to share in new life was when Christ shone forth, since he is the firstfruit of those created into incorruption.
comments.comment: For the fitting time to share in the new and unstained life would be only — and most reasonably — the time when Emmanuel shone forth. Before him no one at all was able to remake us into new life; he himself is like a firstfruit and first of those created into incorruption, inasmuch as he appeared as man and in flesh with us through likeness to us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why nothing may be eaten before the firstfruits are brought.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: Seven weeks counted from the sheaf point to our Pentecost, kept after the resurrection of the Savior.
comments.comment: And at once he has brought in a clear sketch of our holy Pentecost, saying that seven weeks must be counted from the bringing-in of the sheaf. (Lev 23:15-16; Acts 2:1) For after the Savior’s resurrection day, stringing seven weeks together, we who have believed keep the feast.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the counting of seven weeks points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: The evergreen palms picture the delights of paradise, perpetual grace and unfading hope.
comments.comment: “And adornments of palms” (Leviticus 23:40). Through these things it is possible to understand that God apportions to us again in Christ the delights of paradise. The branches of evergreen trees signify in themselves the perpetual nature of grace and the unfading quality of hope.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the branches of the feast of tabernacles signify.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Notes on Leviticus

comments.capsule: The oil of the lamp is pure because the light in the churches comes through Christ by the Spirit, and the single lamp of the first tent shows the lesser light given under the law.
comments.comment:
The oil, then, is pure, and it is olive oil besides: that is, it comes from olives, not from other, more earthy kinds of seed, which did yield pressed oil, but oil that was spurious and, so to speak, adulterated. For the light in the churches is always pure and truly genuine: the light, clearly, that comes through Christ, by the Spirit, even if it is ministered through the voice of the saints, to whom Christ said: ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14). And this is no wonder. For with those whom he called his brothers (Hebrews 2:11) and made partakers of himself (Hebrews 3:14), he would fittingly share the glory of his own honors as well.

So the lamp burns in the first tent as well, and the matter would have a twofold sense. In the inner tent seven lamps shine (Exodus 25:37); they are kindled in the morning, and they pour a rich light upon those who hurry in. And the lampstand was Christ, again as in a type, flooding with abundant and generous light those who wish to hurry into the Holy of Holies. For, it says, ‘Come to him and be enlightened’ (Psalm 34:5). Moreover, the lighting of the lamps in the morning would signify the time when he became man. For something like a day dawned, and a light perceived by the mind shone out, driving away the darkness of our ancient ignorance and scattering the mist that had fallen like night upon the hearts of all. So too the prophet called for the time of the Savior’s coming among us, when he said: ‘In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will keep watch’ (Psalm 5:3). For when would the prayers of all have become acceptable, and when would we who once wandered have stood, as it were, before God, through kinship with him (the spiritual kind, of course) and through obedience and faith, if the light from heaven, that is, Christ, had not shone upon us?

So in the inner tent the light of the seven lamps is rich and clear, but in the first tent it was a single lamp that gave light; and it showed, I think, that not even those being schooled under the law were without the divine light, as the thing itself makes plain. For the law given through Moses also called people out of the worship of many gods to the knowledge of him who is God by nature and in truth. It drew the people of old away from still serving the creation rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25), and persuaded them that they must hold fast to the Maker of all. And these things were not achieved in the souls of those under its schooling without the light perceived by the mind. So, to say it once more, the illumination that comes from Christ is rich and plentiful for those who enter the Holy of Holies, but less for those under the law; and the statement is true.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The lamp is John the Baptist, who went before Christ, and the twelve loaves in two rows are the apostles, who nourish us by sharing in the one Bread from heaven.
comments.comment:
The lamp, perhaps, is John, the inspired Baptist, while the twelve loaves prefigure for us the company of the holy apostles.

Palladius: In what way?

Cyril: Or do you not know that for those under the law in Judea the inspired Baptist was a kind of lamp going before Christ, and that God the Father spoke of him beforehand: ‘I have prepared a lamp for my Christ’ (Psalm 132:17)? The Savior himself also bore witness to this, saying of him to the teachers of the Jews: ‘He was the lamp that burns and shines, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light’ (John 5:35). See how blessed Paul, as one learned in the law, all but calls to mind the lamp in the first tent (Hebrews 9:2). For the lawgiver commanded that it must be kept unquenched, saying: ‘And Aaron and his sons shall burn it from evening until morning before the Lord continually’ (Leviticus 24:3). Yet the Jews took delight in John for a very short time, in that they ran to the baptism he gave and marveled greatly at him; then they put the ever-shining lamp to sleep in death, all but quenching it. For even if the crime may perhaps be called Herod’s (Matthew 14:10), still he was of Israel’s blood. That is why Christ, charging the peoples of the Jews with their insolence against every holy man, says: ‘It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem’ (Luke 13:33). … And in the same way we say that the holy apostles are to be understood as loaves. For only one is bread by nature and in truth: the bread that is from heaven and gives life (John 6:33). But by imitation of the one who is bread by nature, and by sharing in him, the divine guides into the mysteries are loaves that nourish us in godliness, putting into us words of life and driving the famine of ignorance out of the souls of those who believe. The loaves are equal in number to the disciples, for they are twelve, and they are laid in two rows, six on this side, it says, and six on that (Leviticus 24:6), almost as if they stood round in a circle, with the one Bread from heaven, that is, Christ, lying in the middle. And each is of two tenths (Leviticus 24:5), that is, of two perfect measures. For the inspired disciples became perfect in both respects, ready for every good thing, distinguished in deed and in word.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The twelve loaves with frankincense and salt prefigure the apostles, who nourish others as sharers in Christ the bread, with fragrant lives and understanding minds.
comments.comment: The law also prefigured these twelve disciples (Matthew 10:2), and the prophets proclaimed them beforehand. It is written in the Mosaic book: “Take fine flour and make it into twelve loaves, and set them on the pure table before the Lord, and set frankincense and salt on them.” (Leviticus 24:5–7) For the bread that came down from heaven “and gives life to the world” (John 6:33–35) is Christ himself; and by imitation of him the blessed disciples too are called breads. Having become sharers in the one who nourishes us unto eternal life, they also nourish, through their own writings, those who “hunger and thirst for righteousness.” … See the skill of the law: “You shall set frankincense and salt on the breads.” Frankincense is a symbol of fragrance; salt, of mind and understanding. Both were present in the highest degree in the holy apostles. Their life was fragrant — they even said, “We are the fragrance of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:15) to Christ — and they were also all-understanding. That is why they also heard, “You are the salt of the earth.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the twelve loaves, frankincense and salt stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on Matthew

comments.capsule: Frankincense stands for the fragrance of sanctification and salt for understanding, and the loaves set out on the Sabbath are the writings of the apostles given as food to the chosen race.
comments.comment: Frankincense and salt are sprinkled on the loaves (Leviticus 24:7). The frankincense points to the sweet fragrance of sanctification and to the fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:15); the salt hints at understanding. For the word of the saints is not senseless or foolish but, as it is written, seasoned with grace and salt (Colossians 4:6), and it gives grace to those who hear (Ephesians 4:29). Christ also said to them, ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13). The loaves are set out on the Sabbath day as well (Leviticus 24:8). For the day on which the holy apostles were made known is the time of the spiritual Sabbath, that is, the coming of Christ. Because those of Israel did not recognize it, Paul says of them, ‘So then there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God’ (Hebrews 4:9). For they did not enter into his rest, because they did not accept faith (Hebrews 3:18–19). The spiritual and true Sabbath rest, then, is the time when our Savior came to dwell among us. The loaves are set out before the eyes of God, and indeed before the eyes of Israel as well. For ‘you shall set them out,’ he says, ‘on the Sabbath day before the Lord continually, from the sons of Israel’ (Leviticus 24:8). They are before the eyes of God, because he looks on the saints and continually counts them worthy of his care; for ‘the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous,’ it says (Psalm 34:15). They are before the eyes of Israel, because Israel ought to give heed to them and, as it were, fixes on them the eye of the mind, of which the bodily eye would be a type. ‘But they shall belong,’ he says, ‘to Aaron and to his sons, and they shall eat them’ (Leviticus 24:9). For the writings of the holy apostles are set before us as food: before us who have been justified in faith, a holy and sacred race, peoples for his own possession (1 Peter 2:9), chosen and anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The Jubilee of seven weeks of years, with the land at rest, debts cancelled and slaves freed, is a type of the present age, in which lesser sins are paid off.
comments.comment: Seven weeks of years made up the renowned Jubilee for the people of old (Leviticus 25:8–10), in which the land kept sabbath, debts were cancelled, and there was release from slavery; and in the number seven a new life, as it were, began afresh, with the old in a way reaching its completion. These things are types of this present age, which circles round through the seven days and runs past us. In it the penalties for lesser sins are paid off, in keeping with the loving care of the good Master, so that we may not be handed over to punishment in the endless age.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Jubilee and what it signifies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Letter to Bishop Optimus

comments.capsule: The house in a walled city, redeemable only within the year, is Israel, which must recover its lot at the coming of the Savior, and the unwalled villages are the nations, which can be redeemed at any time.
comments.comment: [Those of Israel, like dwellers in a city] … that is walled and girded about with help from above, who have the minds of townsfolk and have not been ignorant of what pleases God, but then disregarded what was fitting, have thrown away through carelessness the lot assigned to them and have fallen from their high hope: unless they sober up from their drunkenness, as it is written (Joel 1:5), and recover what is their own while the year of redemption is here (Leviticus 25:29–30), that is, the coming of our Savior, they will be left as they are from then on and will be subject forever to the buyer, that is, to Satan. ‘For behold,’ he says, ‘you were sold for your iniquities, and for your sins I sent away your mother’ (Isaiah 50:1). But the multitude of the nations, wholly without help and sick with a rustic and untaught mind, and for that reason driven out into slavery under others, can be redeemed at any time (Leviticus 25:31), because God takes pity on it. For it will take back its own lot, called to freedom in the year of release, when Christ set free all the earth under the sun from the greed of the demons, rescued it from the snares of sin, justified it by faith and sanctified it in the Spirit, canceling by his own cross the bond that stood against us (Colossians 2:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the one year of redemption for town houses and the open redemption of village houses stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: A house in a walled town could be redeemed only for a year, but fields and the Levites' houses could be redeemed at any time, since the Levites' portion was their lot.
comments.comment: Listen, then. When people buy buildings in a town from their owners, the sellers, it says, may refund what they were given, for up to one year. If this does not happen, then once the year has passed, let the buyer be the owner, it says, and from then on beyond any written claim. But if it is a field and a farmstead, let it be allowed, it says, to recover it at any time, once the one who sold it has paid back to the buyer the money he was given. If he cannot pay it back and recover the property, the law commanded that it be released in the fiftieth year, without the former owner paying anything. For the law credited the buyer of the property with the profits of the long period as repayment of what was owed. These things God laid down for the common people. But the Levites’ holdings he set apart once more, as it were, in an honor of their own, saying that they are redeemable at all times and forbidding them to be sold: ‘For this,’ it says, ‘is their portion and lot’ (Leviticus 25:34).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The Levites’ possessions can never be sold off, because the lot of the saints is kept safe and their hope stands firm in Christ.
comments.comment: The possessions of the Levites, however, can never be sold off (Leviticus 25:32–34); for the lot is kept safe for the saints, and their hope stands firm. So it was that Christ once said of Mary, who was so very eager to learn, that she had chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her (Luke 10:42). Yet for small and great, for priest and people, and in a word for all, redemption and the security of hope are in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Levites’ possessions can never be sold.
