comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Constant meditation on the law carries us straight and drives away forgetfulness, and the lawgiver adds hope of blessings as bait to encourage the doing of it.
comments.comment: Therefore the long and continual meditation of the law carries away unto the straight—and this would be what seems to God—sending out forgetfulness as it were some turbid thing and mist of a human’s understanding. And the lawgiver does not stop unto these things, but inventing also something better besides, he makes hope as it were some bait of the eagerness at least in needing to do—the hope upon all the most prayed-for things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: The law's blessing that the righteous man eats and is filled speaks of the food of the soul, which alone is filled, and does not contradict the Gospel's warning against anxiety.
comments.comment:
Nor, again, are these sayings contrary to the blessings in the Law, which teach that the righteous man eats and is filled (compare Leviticus 26:5; Deuteronomy 11:15): “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will drink. Consider the birds of the air,” or, “Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, and our heavenly Father feeds them. How much more do you surpass the birds?” (Matthew 6:25–26; Luke 12:24), and “Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field” (Matthew 6:28), and what follows. Nor are they contrary to what Solomon said in these words: “A righteous man eats and fills his soul, but the souls of the ungodly are in want” (Proverbs 13:25).

For we must see that the blessing in the Law makes known the food of the soul, with which it is not the composite man that is filled, but the soul alone. From the Gospel, however, we should perhaps take something deeper, and perhaps also something simpler: that one must not let the soul be distracted by cares about food and clothing, but, practising plain living, be confident of being provided for by God, if one takes thought only for what is necessary.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the promise that the righteous will eat and be filled means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VII

comments.capsule: Writings that seem to put God in a bodily place are to be read as his dwelling and walking in the saints, and so too he dwells in heaven, that is, in every saint and in Christ.
comments.comment: And since, even before Christ's bodily sojourn, many writings seem to say God is in a bodily place, it seems to me not out of place to set out a few of those as well, to remove all entanglement from those who, through boorishness, enclose the God over all in a small and narrow place, so far as they can. … let us sufficiently recall the 'I will dwell in them and walk in them,' (Leviticus 26:12) said by God in Deuteronomy. For whatever his walk among the saints is, such too is the walk in Paradise — with God hiding, and everyone who sins fleeing his oversight and falling from frankness. … As, then, he dwells in the saints, so also in heaven — that is, in every saint and in Christ, in whom are all the saved as 'luminaries' and stars of heaven …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Prayer

comments.capsule: God measures punishments with mercy, adding them stage by stage, because he desires to lead the transgressor to repentance and not wholly destroy him.
comments.comment: The one judging the condemned grants place and does not immediately bear the end of punishment upon the transgressor. Therefore, 'judging briefly, he punishes.' This is exemplified in Leviticus, where prior punishments are recorded before subsequent penalties. The Lord says, 'If you do not turn back, I will add seven more plagues.' (Leviticus 26:18) Another punishment is again described: 'If you do not turn back, but go astray, I will go with you in a sideways manner.' (Leviticus 26:23-24) You will find God measuring punishments with mercy, as He desires to lead the transgressor to repentance, not wholly destroying them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the penalties in Leviticus 26 come in stages.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Homilies on Jeremiah

comments.capsule: The seven plagues are inflicted one by one, and not all are struck with seven, for some are struck with one, two or more according to what God knows.
comments.comment: I consider that for us also such things may be, and some punishments may occur, so that these may not have a second punishment but be satisfied with the first, others may come even to the second, not indeed to the third, others may come even to the fourth. For the 'I will add seven plagues' (Leviticus 26:21) signifies a mystery of one by one being inflicted, and the second, and the third, up to the seven mentioned for some. Not all are struck with seven plagues; rather, some I suppose will be struck with seven, others with five, others with four, others with three or two, and the most helpless among all in punishments I consider to be struck with one. Therefore, God knows the things regarding the plagues.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Homilies on Jeremiah

comments.capsule: The seven plagues for walking crookedly came upon those who denied the seven gifts of the Spirit, and the wild beasts are the nations who now rule them.
comments.comment:
“And if after this you walk crookedly” (Leviticus 26:21): for they never kept their heart straight toward God, and far less in the later times, when they swerved from the call of Christ. Therefore he went on: “And if you will not obey me” – and indeed they did not obey when Christ called – “I will bring seven more plagues on you according to your lawless deeds” (Leviticus 26:21). For since they denied the seven gifts of the Spirit, the seven spirits of wickedness, which entered and dwelt in them, become seven plagues for them; and their last state became worse than the first (Matthew 12:45).

“And I will send against you the wild beasts of the earth” (Leviticus 26:22). He means the nations; for formerly, through their ignorance, they were beasts, because they worshiped the divine in the image of beasts and four-footed creatures and reptiles (Romans 1:23). Cursing them, David said: “May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). These are the nations God has now sent against them, and they do what the lawgiver says next: “And they shall devour you, and consume your cattle, and make you few; and your roads shall be deserted” (Leviticus 26:22). For every one of these things has happened to them, both visibly and spiritually, since they have been ruled by the nations.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Saint Stephen

comments.capsule: Those who turn away from God hear that he will go against them, but God is not made less by their leaving, as the sun is not, and they only harm themselves.
comments.comment:
And of the man being with God, and God being with him: it has been said: 'Draw near to God and he will draw near to you' (Jas 4:8); but when some turn away from him, they hear: 'They went astray from me, and I will go to them in angry wrath' (Leviticus 26:28).

And just as the one leaving the sun and closing his eyes does not do anything to make the sun less—for it remains as it was, shining—so the one leaving God works harm upon himself; and he leaves him not as if in a place, but turning away from virtue, as those about whom it has been said: 'God will cast them off, because they did not listen to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Dt 32:19); for because they themselves did not listen, he cast them off.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God will walk contrary to those who leave him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: On Genesis

comments.capsule: The valuations by age and sex measure the spiritual fruit each can bring, from the prime of life to the infant in Christ, for whom milk is the fitting food.
comments.comment: According to what the history suggests, these would be the people from twenty years old up to sixty (Leviticus 27:3). For up to the sixtieth year the body stays strong and at its most vigorous in its movements. By then the mind, too, is settled and in a way strong, and it is very well suited to take in whatever it chooses to learn. And he who knows our frame, as it is written (Psalm 103:14), surely knew that there is such an age in souls also. For the passage, no doubt, moves, by likenesses drawn from bodily things, to the things perceived by the mind. So, whether one is male or female, let those who are still in the prime of that inward age bring what has been appointed. That is, let the male bring, in the form, as it were, of fifty didrachms, the fruit of spiritual worship, sound and as perfect as can be; for by way of seven times seven it is plainly seen to reach the highest goal and to be attested as perfect. The female, again, brings it in the form, as it were, of thirty didrachms (Leviticus 27:4). For she is held in less esteem than the male, yet she still brings, in keeping with her own nature, a fruit marked by perfection and toil, as the three tens suggest. The one from five years old up to twenty, if male, pays twenty didrachms; if female, ten (Leviticus 27:5). For from the age of five, I think, and barely then, the mind begins in a way to open its eyes, as it were, to understanding. That understanding is still childish and weak, but it is moving toward the better, and the body is growing ever stronger. … So the fruit from each person is measured in proportion to spiritual strength. Everywhere the female comes after the male, and often at half. For the inspired Paul has plainly testified that the vessel is weak (1 Peter 3:7). She falls short of the natural ability of men, and she keeps silent in the churches (1 Corinthians 14:34). For she has not been entrusted with the word, and she is by no means as strong for achieving virtue as the male is seen to be. From one month old, it says, up to five years, the male gives five didrachms, and the female, for her part, three (Leviticus 27:6). And yet what fruit could come from infants? So in a way the passage hints to us at the newborn child in Christ, those for whom, as the holy Paul said, milk is the fitting food (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: God asks of each in proportion to his measure, accepting what a person can afford, and in this he sends away none who come to him by faith.
comments.comment: Look, then, at the matter as it is written in the law, and see God asking of each in proportion to each one’s measure. Being the spring and source of a gentleness and love for humankind beyond words, he sends away none of those who have run to him through faith; he welcomes each with whatever he has, and accepts spiritual offerings, in every case excusing what lies beyond a person’s strength. … For some came forward, enrolling themselves with God for consecration and as an offering dedicated to him, and gladly dedicating the sum of didrachms the law had fixed. But if someone was not very well off, that is, one of the humbler sort, the payment was no longer made by the legal scale; instead the priest serving at the time assessed him, and a debt matched to his means was set. This, then, is the plainer account and sense of the letter.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: God, who is just and compassionate, accepts fruit in proportion to each person's zeal and capacity, measuring what he asks of the weak by their strength.
comments.comment: [Those of sixty years and over] … could hardly be very fruitful, just as aging plants, when their root grows old, are seen to be slow in putting forth ripe fruit. So God, who is truly just and loves to show compassion, accepts the fruits in proportion to each person’s zeal and capacity of mind. He neither disregards what is feeble and past its prime, sending it away as powerless, nor lets the strong go without reward; rather he opens wide, as it were, the way for those who are willing to win his approval, in whatever manner each is able. And those who are weaker in their condition, and perhaps also of little understanding, he himself will keep, measuring the fruit he asks of each by his strength. For this, I think, is the meaning of: ‘He shall stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him according to what the one who vowed can afford’ (Leviticus 27:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the priest values the poor man according to what he can afford.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16
